In the absence of the member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Lafortune) I beg to move for leave to introduce Bill No. 52. to amend the Criminal Code.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Explain.

The folowing section is inserted immediately after Section 229 of the Criminal Code, Chapter 146 of the Revised Statutes of Canada:
229a. Everyone is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to two years imprisonment or a penalty not exceeding one hundred dollars, or both, who
(a)	In any premises under his control, to which the public have access, engages in or petmits other persons to engage in the game known as "Three Card Monte" or similar game played with other instruments than cards,
(b)	Engages in the game of Three Card Monte, or similar game played with other instruments than cards, in any public place, or any place to which the public have access.
The member for Jacques Cartier himself could explain the Bill more fully than I can. It has for its object,. however, the preventing of the extortion of money from people in the city of Montreal through the carrying on of a crooked confidence game which has been flourishing there for some time. The law does not seem to be very clear on this subject; the courts have had difficulty in finding any authority upon which to base the conviction of- culprits who have been found guilty of engaging in this practice.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext: Not upon the Orders of the Day. The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Trade and Commerce-Canada Grain Act, administration ot, $1,175,000.
['There is a Bill under way.']
Will the minister explain the increase of $175,000?

This appropriation covers the operations under the supervision of the Board of Grain Commissioners in carrying out the operations authorized under the Canada Grain Act. The increase of $175,000 over last year is almost, if not entirely, due to reclassification and the raising of salaries consequent thereupon. This appropriation covers all expenditures for salaries of officials, permanent and temporary, and contingencies of the various officers under the eastern and western grain inspection division; it includes salaries and contingencies of the Board of Grain Commissioners, the working expenses of all Government elevators, internal and at port terminals, and salaries and expenses of the grain research laboratory, with the exception of the chief chemist, who is on the Civil Service list and whose salary has already been passed.
I may say generally with reference to this service that it is self-sustaining, and a little more than that, varying from year to year according to the crop. For the year 1920-1921 up to January 31, the fees collected amounted to $1,118,813, which is a little larger than the revenue for the whole year 1919-1920, so that we may expect to find, when the accounts are closed to the 31st of March, that the total receipts for the year have been considerably above those of the previous year; and if we have as

good a crop next season the revenues on the same basis will meet the expenditure and probably leave something to the good. The aim is, as far as possible, to make the service pay its way. During the several years that the Grain Act has been in operation there have been years when there was a deficit, but since 1911 I have tried so to arrange it that whilst the charges shall not be so high as to bring in a great surplus, they shall be sufficient to meet the expenditure for the year, and leave a little surplus to go upon in case the returns for the following year are not so large.
How many grain elevators has the Government?

The Government has a terminal elevator at Port Arthur, terminal elevators at Saskatoon, Moosejaw and Calgary, and a transfer elevator in Vancouver. There is also a bit of the foundation of an elevator in futuro at Hudson Bay, but that is not in operation at present so far as elevating grain is concerned.

Are there any in the
East?

The Government has elevators in the East at Port Colborne, operated by the railway department in connection with the railways, as well as elevators under the Harbour Commissioners in Montreal and Quebec. Then there is a small elevator in Halifax, which is in fact a transfer elevator.

The Quebec elevator is
not very busy, is it?

It has done
some work, and I hope it will be busier in the future.
Would the minister explain the increase of $175,000 in this item?

My hon. friend's question shows he was too busy conversing with his mate, because I have answered exactly the same question by the leader of the Opposition. I am not averse, however, to answering it again. The increase of $175,000 is due to the increases in salaries under re-classification. Altogether, under this vote some 429 employees are paid, so the increases spread over that number amount to a pretty tidy sum.

I understand the country derives some revenue from this

item. Where can we find a statement of that?
I can give my hon. friend the figures.

Are they not
published?
I already gave them when my hon. friend was conversing.
What is the amount to be expended on the Quebec elevator out of this item?

Nothing has
been expended on the Quebec elevator by us. It was built by the Harbour Commissioners of Quebec, out of loans advanced by the Dominion Government. The elevator is managed by the commission.
Has the Government nothing to do with its management?
No.
The minister has given the elevators in the West and in the province of Quebec. How many are there in the Maritime Provinces?

I gave that
information, but I will give it again. There is a small elevator at Halifax, used chiefly for transfer purposes. That is the only one the Government owns in the Maritime Provinces. The Government had an elevator, as my hon. friend will recollect, in St. John, but it was destroyed by fire. The Canadian Pacific have elevators on the west side, which do the grain transfer of the harbour.
Are the revenues pertaining to this item published in the Trade and Commerce report?
Yes, I will give them to my hon. friend. The revenue for 1920-1921 up to January 31, was $1,118,813.

How does that compare
with the expenditure?

The expendi-
* ture that is asked to be voted for the coming year is $1,175,000. The expenditure up to January 31, 1921, was $982,431, but of course the accounts are not all in for the year ending to-day, nor even for the period up to January 31. The expenditure so far as the accounts have come in, is quite a bit less than the revenue up to January 31. There is no doubt that the
revenue for the year ending to-day will be over and above the expenditure.
Does the minister follow the financial year or the calendar year in adjusting these accounts?

The financial
year.

I should like some information from the minister in connection with an answer which was given yesterday by the Minister of Finance to a question I asked. My question was, what were the approved securities forming part of the basis on which a large number of Dominion notes were issued. Dominion notes are authorized up to a certain number of millions of dollars, according to the gold kept in the vault. A change has been made in the statute by which not only gold but securities forming part of the basis on issue of Dominion notes. The question was, what are the particular securities on which this $127,000,000 of Dominion notes are issued? The Minister of Finance tells us that, among other things, Dominion of Canada bonds were one of the securities, others being bonds of the Canadian National Railways and assignments of grain and produce. How can grain and produce be used as a basis of currency in Canada?
What is the last phrase my hon. friend is reading?

A number of securities are specified, among others, assignments of grain and produce and demand notes of commercial houses endorsed by banks to the order of the Minister of Finance. Now, it was a new idea to me that grain and produce could be used as a basis of issue of notes for circulation in Canada. We were accustomed to the idea that Dominion notes must be based on gold, and I confess it was a rather startling idea to me that bonds of the Canadian Government,-a debt owed by the Government itself-could be used as a basis for the issue of further notes. That, however, is not the question I am asking now. The question is: By what means are grain and produce used as a basis for issuing Dominion notes?

I am not entirely conversant with the matter. The Minister of Finance will give more precise information to my hon. friend. But I suppose

that these are bankers' securities that they hold. It does not mean that grain in its passage through Canada can be, or is, in any way used as a basis lor the issue of Dominion notes. It must mean that notes are issued on the strength of securities which the bankers have. However, I would prefer my hon. friend to take the matter up with the Minister of Finance.

Will the minister please explain these items contained on page Z 12 of the Auditor General's report?
* Advances to George Searls, chief inspector, Winnipeg, $115,711. Advances to George Searls, chief inspector, Winnipeg, $129,445.57.
It seems that the Auditor General's report does not afford much information with regard to the expenditure of this money.

My hon. friend will quite understand the purpose of these advances. Mr. Searls is chief inspector of the whole of the grain business and has a large staff at Winnipeg working under him. All the samplers, graders, inspectors and clerks who have to carry on this manifold work must be paid, and an advance is put into the bank to the credit of Mr. Searls. When these salary cheques become due he checks out against that advance.

His own personal
cheques?

No, the
cheques are all official. It may be that his is the last signature, but the cheques are thoroughly conserved as to security.
Are all these employees under Civil Service Commission appointment?
They are all under Civil Service Commission appointment except those that are not.
Oh, oh!

That statement sounds superfluous, no doubt, but I will explain the situation to my hon. friend. Those that are not under the Civil Service Commission are nevertheless under a certain regulation; according to the income of the grain at different seasons, or at different periods within active seasons, it is necessary to put on a certain number of temporary employees. Similarly, if a man goes out through sickness or any other cause someone must be put in his place. Now, it is obviously impossible to carry on these operations uninterruptedly if a written request for employees to fill these tem-

porary positions must be sent to the Civil Service Commission. If such written applications were sent to the commission, the positions would have to be advertised, and that, of course, would consume so much time that in the interval the service would be disorganized. Under an arrangement with the Civil Service Commission, the staff officer out there, Mr. Searls, can put on these temporary employees as the necessity for them arises. They cannot be termed permanent because, after a little time, the rush is over and their services are immediately dispensed with. Trouble having become imminent in regard to temporary positions, I requested the Civil Service Commission to send one of their number to Winnipeg. He went into the whole matter with the authorities there, and this arrangement was agreed upon between them and is being carried out under the supervision of the Commission.

What is the system that
prevails in the appointment of these temporary employees?
I cannot give complete information regarding the whole modus operandi.

Is it similar to the
system in connection with the census?
No.
What is the difference?

I know nothing about the matter so far as the temporary employees are concerned, neither do any of my officers. If Mr. Searls wants a man for any of the reasons I have given, he employs a proper individual who, in his judgment, is fitted for the work. These appointments are absolutely without the least shadow of patronage so far as my department or anybody else is concerned. They are within the entire control of the supervising officer himself.
Who is one of the officers under my right.hon. friend?
Yes; if he were not he would not be there.

Then I am sure this gentleman will take into his serious consideration the advices he receives from my right hon. friend's supporter, the member for the particular locality, when he makes such appointments.

I am quite sure, because I have absolute knowledge, that

he acts on no recommendations, he takes recommendations from no person whatever. Any one may submit a name to him, but he acts entirely on his own responsibility. I hope my hon. friend will be serious about this matter.
I am.

Two hundred and fifty thousand cars pass through that centre. They have their periods of congestions as also of diminished numbers, and Mr. Searls is absolutely responsible for getting these cars graded and checked through with the very minimum of delay. He is responsible for the grades, because they furnish the basis upon which commercial transactions go on. Being responsible, therefore, he is the only man to decide who these temporary employees shall be.
Does he also settle the question of salaries or remuneration?

The question
of remuneration is settled, under those circumstances, on the basis of the current wage for that kind of employment in the locality. That is the wage he pays. But he must have the men, he must carry on the work; and if he cannot get a man that suits him at that wage, he is at liberty to give him what is necessary. And this has the approval of the Civil Service Commission.
What opportunity has he for making a comparison with the wage that is paid elsewhere for similar work?

Mr. Searls is in the very centre of the grain business. He has been there, as my hon. friend knows, for a long period of years. He knows what an expert grader gets, and what the current wage is, and I do not know of any person in Winnipeg who would have a deeper or more comprehensive knowledge than he would in regard to the services for which he requires men.

I quite agree with what my right hon. friend has said because I know Mr. Searls intimately. But my point has reference to the minister's statement that Mr. Searls paid the current wage. Now there is no other similar work being carried on in the city of Winnipeg that I know of-there is only the one inspection bureau.

My hon. friend must surely be a little bit mistaken in that
statement as regards men who are competent to grade grain. The work done in the other elevators, and by the other companies, gives Mr. Searls a line upon which he can base his determination. But outside of that, he knows the man he wants and he gets him by giving him what he considers necessary to obtain his services and to keep them. He also knows thoroughly well the wages that are current in ether cities, outside of Canada itself, where graders are used. I do not know any one who would know the facts in that regard better than he.

I quite admit that Mr. Searls is quite qualified to estimate the ability of the man he is employipg, but he has no other similar institution, such as there is elsewhere, which will enable him to make a comparison as to the wages that are paid-there is only the one inspection bureau in Winnipeg. It is different in other places. For example they have an independent inspection bureau on the other side of the line. That is something that we have for a long time been trying to get this Government to establish, but so far without success. I believe there should be a check maintained in that respect. That is why I raise the point.
While we are on the matter of inspection I would like to draw attention to another point. When the salaries in connection with the Grain Act, were under consideration a short time ago the stipend of the individual in charge of the laboratory in Winnipeg was under review. The hour was rather late and I did not press the point at that time, but I now wish to have a little further elucidation. The point arose in connection with the amount of moisture that was allowed in the grain to permit it to enter certain grades. If 1 remember correctly the minister said that that factor did not enter into the matter of grading to any extent-that the grading was done by the feel, the touch, and the appearance and colour of the grain. In reality the operation of grading goes much further. I believe there is a fixed standard and that 12.8 of moisture is permitted in the grain. Now we in the West have never been able, as yet, to find out just who has been responsible for the fixing of that amount of moisture which is permitted in the grain, other than the chief inspector. No doubt that official takes advice from other individuals. And that is where our quarrel arose. I remember

that at a sitting of the Grain Commission held in Winnipeg a few years ago this point came up. We always believed, and experience has proved, that the amount of moisture allowed in grain to enable it to enter storage in certain grades is much below	the	amount	of moisture	thatgrain	will	carry	and keep.	Thathas	been	proved	before; but	at
the sitting in question representatives of the two largest milling concerns in Canada were present and they were much opposed to the amount of moisture being increased -that is the amount of moisture allowed in the different standards of grain. They claimed that they were continuously having trouble in disposing of their flour to the European buyers on account of the excess of moisture that was in the flour. We, as producers, were absolutely helpless in the face of that argument advanced by two responsible men. However, I took opportunity on the very first occasion that offered to make a little inquiry into the matter. I happened to be in the office of another of the largest milling concerns in Canada, who also have interests in the United States. I asked the manager of this firm if they were exporting large quantities of flour to the Old Country, and he replied in the affirmative. I then asked him if they had any difficulty or any complaint as to the amount of moisture that was contained in their flour, and he replied that they had absolutely never heard of a single complaint from any person. Now that mill was running day and night, including Sundays, on war orders, continuously during the war; and yet those people had received absolutely no complaint at all as to any excess of moisture in their flour milled from practically the same wheat as the other mills were milling from the different concerns' elevators being scattered over the entire country. Now that is our complaint. There is a difference of anywhere from six to eight and ten cents a bushel in the price paid for grain, as between the straight grade and what is known as "tough." The mills are usually quite anxious to get the grain that is graded tough, as I think the reports of the chemist in Winnipeg if they are examined will show that that grade makes just as good wheat for milling purposes and can be used to as good advantage as even the straight grade. The only difference is the actual weight of the excess of moistureone-half, one-quarter, or one per cent_______
which it may contain.
Has not the wheat got to be passed through a drier, which is an advantage?

No it does not have to be passed through a drier; it is simply run in with the other grain and there is no drying process-in fact moisture is added to it. Those who understand the milling business know that moisture has to be added to wheat in order to fit it for a proper working. Under the circumstances we would like to have this matter investigated a little further. We do not think that the man who is in charge of the inspection should say just what amount of moisture wheat should contain before it is permitted to enter certain grades. We are especially fortified in that opinion by reason of the evidence given at the sitting to which I alluded, where it was clearly shown that the inspector based his conclusions on the statement of the millers alluded to-statements which were absolutely contradicted by another firm who have practically as large milling interests, and as large an European market, as are possessed by those who appeared before the commission. I would like the minister to take this matter into consideration, as it means a very heavy loss to the farmers of western Canada for no reason whatever.
Carried.

Before the vote carries
I notice an item of $350,000 of revenue from the surplus fund of the Board of Grain Supervisors of Canada. I would like to know just how that money has been apportioned? Has it been allotted to assist in meeting the expense of the administration of the Canada Grain Act, or has it gone into the general revenue?
My hon. friend refers to the surplus that was left over after the Board of Grain Supervisors had finished their work?
Yes.
That went into the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
I would like to know if that is the only surplus that has gone into that fund from the handling of grain under the control of the Government at different times.

Yes. The surplus which remained, after all the accounts have been adjusted and the expenses pro-

vided for, went into the Consolidated Revenue Fund. The wheat board has been in charge during the succeeding season, and there will be a certain surplus over and above the expenses after the distribution of the $2.63 a bushel which has already gone into the farmers' hands. That surplus, however, is so small that it is absolutely impracticable to make a division of it amongst the holders of certificates

the expense of making the distribution would be almost as great as the amount to be distributed. But any small surplus will go into Consolidated Revenue Fund. As to whether there are any other surpluses, there were no other methods that i know of by which any could accrue to the Government on the handling of grain. My hon. friend may have sometning in mind, and if he mentions it I will be able to tell him clearly.
Was there any surplus from the first commandeering Ox certain quantities of wheat at the head of the lakes?
My impression is there was none. I will make inquiries and let my hon. friend know.
Am I right in understanding that this large increase of $175,000 in this vote is to provide for salaries under the reclassification?
Yes, that increase arises from reclassification.
What percentage of the total cost of administration is attributable to salaries?	[DOT]
I can give my hon. friend 1919-1920, which is a full year.
That is satisfacory.

The statement of expenditure for that year is as follows: Board of Grain Commissioners, salaries $21,200, wages, commissions and contingencies $9,522, making a total for the Board of Grain Commissioners and their staff of $30,722. In the western inspection division the salaries amounted to $219,300; wages and contingencies, $340,389, making a total of $559,691. In the eastern inspection division the total is $13,411. And in the Grain Research Laboratory the total is $9,244. Therefore the total for permanent salaries is $256,052, and for wages and contingencies $357,018, or together $613,070, the total expense of the Act being $925,597.

One hundred anu seventy-five thousand dollars seems a very large increase on a little over six hundred thousand dollars. It would appear as though the Civil Service Commision was a rather expensive institution if its reclassification has resulted in similar increase an the way through.
My hon. friend will recollect that there are about 400 employees altogether, including temporary and permanent.

That does not affect the percentage. That percentage is tremendously high. It would be interesting to have comparative results in the case of a similar number of employees in any other department. We have heard both in the House and in the press a good deal about the appointment of a commission of inquiry into the grain trade. Will the expense of that inquiry be taken care of by these figures?
That would not come under these figures at all.

Of course, the appointment of that commission comes,
4 p.m. indirectly at least, from the Department of Trade and Commerce?
I presume so.

The personnel of that commission is of great interest to us in the West; in fact, the whole inquiry depends on the personnel. I do not know whether we are to pay attention to current rumours or not, but if some of the men whose names are mentioned are to be on that commission, the expenditure entailed will be absolutely thrown away. Among the names mentioned are those of two gentlemen, one a direct member and the other was secretary for years. The most important feature that needs investigation, it seems to me, is the working of that Grain Commission. Certain transactions we would like to have an opportunity of probing, for instance, the famous Curry case-11,000 bushels of wheat went out of one government elevator without anybody knowing anything about it. Now, the Grain Commission is absolutely responsible there, and in the investigation or suit entered to determine the ownership of this quantity of wheat in so far as I can find, not a single individual who had to do with the moving of that wheat from the elevator was called on the carpet. There are other things we would like to inquire into as well.

My hon. friend will have a full opportunity of criticising

the commission when it is appointed, and maybe it would be just as well to wait until that time, as then we will be certain we are criticising the proper parties.

I am not criticising the proposed commission, I am criticising the grain commission that has been in existence for years. To my mind there is absolutely no use in appointing a commission to inquire into the irregularities that have been mentioned across the floor of the House if the personnel of that commission is to include gentlemen who were or are connected with the Grain Commission which is responsible for some of those irregularities. If there is anything in the rumours I have referred to, the commission certainly will not appeal to the grain trade and the wheat producers in Western Canada.
We will see when the report comes out.

Although we are not a grain producing country in Cape Breton we are very much interested in grain and its products, and I would like some further information on the grain question. The minister has been congratulated that notwithstanding the many changes which have taken place in the ministry which he adorns, his own department has been managed so satisfactorily by him that he has continued to remain at its head. For that reason we appeal to him with all the greater confidence for reliable information. I must congratulate the minister upon being able to give information which, whether or not it is always well founded, is pretty well rounded off and stands the test for the time being. Many years ago I suggested that the minister's department should be able to follow the grain through its various stages from the time it left the field until it got into the hands of the consumer and to be able at all times to tell the people whether or not they were getting a square deal. The price of flour at present is abnormal. For many years we got the very best flour available for $5 a barrel, sometimes for $4.50, but now we are paying as high as $16 a barrel, although the income of many men who have to buy that flour is pretty much at a standstill. The people who pay that big price expect their representatives in Parliament to ascertain some of the facts in connection with this very important staple article. I heard the minister say yesterday that the price of wheat had gone down very materially. Is that reduction in the price of

wheat to be followed by a reduction in the price of flour? A western man who is very much interested in this business told me the other day that figuring a fair price for flour and counting four and one-half bushels of wheat to a barrel, flour should sell at $8 or $8.50 a barrel. Now, there is an enormous profit somewhere when a barrel which, it is stated, should sell at $8.50 or thereabouts actually sells at $16. The ordinary person has no power to inquire into these things. During the war the people were told that they could complain to their town council or municipal council of any exhorbitant charges made for the necessities of life, with a view to having the matter taken before a magistrate's court. That procedure was not of much avail; it was not productive of any serious results. These things must be dealt with by the machinery of government, and if it is a fact that the price of wheat has gone down and that wages are to some extent going down, the Department of Trade and Commerce should at least make it known authoritatively that there is no justification for these exorbitant and as it would appear to me extortionate, prices of flour. I am well informed that we have no honest competition in any trade in this country; that everything is divided off and that a combine of more or less potentiality exists with respect to all these things. The Government has cut off the head of the Board of Oommerce; therefore they have taken the responsibility upon themselves. I bring these matters in all seriousness to the minister's attention in the hope that there shall be no combines, either in connection with grain or the activities of the millers or the wholesaling and retailing of flour, which will make possible the charging of extortionate prices. No one finds fault with the carrying on of business in a proper way and with a view to making legitimate profits, but the people do object to any combine which has the effect of restricting production and keeping up prices. I am sure that the minister has such a knowledge of his department as will enable him to take this matter in hand. It is not one which concerns me personally, because the quantity of flour I buy is very small.
The hon. gentleman eats oats mostly.

Yes, I am largely an
oats eater. I commend it to my right hon. friend or to anyone else, because it produces the proper kind of pugnacious material. As I say, I bring these matters to the attention of the minister in all serious-

ness on behalf of thousands of people who buy flour and have families to feed.

Following up the
remarks of the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) may I ask the minister if it is the intention of the Government to appoint a commission to inquire into the grain trade of this country?

There have
been rumours that such is in the air, but I think all I can say to my hon. friend is that if a commission is to be appointed, announcement will be made to the House in due course. I cannot give him any other information.

Judging from the
minister's answer a commission may or may not be appointed. I think there is no need for such a commission, because the present grain board have every power to investigate all matters pertaining to the grain trade. Why another commission should be appointed at great cost to the country is more than I can understand. Rumour also has it that in connection with the personnel of this commission the name of a member of the present board is mentioned. If anything of that kind is done it would only tend to create dissatisfaction and no good results would be obtained. The appointment of a new commission to deal with matters pertaining to the grain trade, would not, I am sure, meet with the approval of the producers of Western Canada. Unless it is an absolutely independent commission.

I quite agree that an independent commission should be appointed to investigate the whole matter. For instance, it would be very interesting for the farmers of Western Canada to know why, when the British Government was buying wheat in June last, they could not buy any in Canada, but they bought a whole year's supply in the United States at $3 a bushel, and then when there was no one buying wheat for Great Britain, how it was that wheat was sold short in Chicago and who benefited by that selling short. Those are matters involving $100,000,000. It is of far more importance to the western farmer to have those facts brought out than to have the duty on a binder reduced by fifty cents. Those are matters that should be investigated because, through some person's action, the markets of the world have virtually been closed to Canada, and a great deal of loss has resulted to the farming community, not only in the West, but in Ontario, and we
ought to know those facts. I quite agree that no one connected with the ring in the West should be put on any of those commissions. Ontario farmers would like to know why they have to pay a toll on their grain to carry wheat for gentlemen in the West. The Ontario farmer has been taxed so much a bushel for all his grain

I do not know whether he is now-to carry wheat in western elevators. Those are matters affecting farmers in the eastern part of the country; an independent commission would go quite a long distance in straightening out these facts, and the Grain Growers' Company of the West should be the first to welcome an investigation, because there have been some ugly rumours in the East with regard to the conduct of their business.

How are the Canadian
farmers taxed?

That is what I should
like to know. The Ontario farmer was charged two cents a bushel all during the war. He does not carry his grain in an elevator, but there was an elevator charge on all the wheat he sold.

I think the hon. member will find that that was in the case of grain sold to the mills. There was some dissatisfaction at the start in connection with that, but I think that matter was gradually straightened out. In reply to the first part of the hon. member's remarks, I think I can tell him why the market was closed to Canada. Immediately on the announcement that the Canada Wheat Board would not be continued for another year, the Americans sold their entire surplus of wheat to Great Britain. That was something they would not have dared to do had the wheat board been continued, as they would have known they would have the wheat board to buy from and not a hundred thousand farmers scattered throughout the country. That is the secret of the whole thing, and the hon. member's estimate of $100,000,000 is quite conservative. In my speech in the debate on the Address I stated that we had lost a hundred million dollars and that our adverse balance of trade between Canada and the United States would have been rectified to that extent, had we had the price we would have had if the wheat board had been continued. That is the answer to the whole thing. Immediately the announcement was made that the wheat board would be discontinued, the Americans sold their surplus



wheat, knowing they could well replace it, and the Chicago market tells the tale. It was pounded down immediately after that; our markets had to follow, and the result was the Americans got at least $100,000,000 of our good money that we should have got from them for our wheat through the one action of the wheat board being discontinued.

The hon. gentleman
knows more about this question than I do.
I am speaking from information. My knowledge of the facts is simply this, that the hon. gentleman and his followers in the grain exchange in the West have been fighting for open markets and free trade for years. They fought the Government last year, and then the action of the Government in regard to the wheat question turned out to be all right. Last year I challenged the hon. member, as a matter of protection, to fix a price for the farmers, and he refused to do so. This year they fought for an open market and they got it. What happened? Great Britain came into the market last June to buy her wheat, but there was no person in Canada to sell our wheat to her. If we had had a grain board, it could have sold the whole Canadian crop for $3 a bushel, but there was no one functioning for Canada. Then the British buyers went to the United States, and they could get people in that country who sold them 180,000,000 bushels in June last. That shut out the Canadian farmer from foreign markets except in the United States. Then these gentlemen, knowing that the needs of the market had been fulfilled as regards the United States' and Canada's crop, and knowing that the British would not be buyers for six months, pounded the market; the grain gamblers in Winnipeg sold fall wheat in Chicago at from $2.80 to $3 a bushel, and then they turned round and hammered the western farmer and covered their trades at around $1.50 a bushel, pocketing the difference. An investigation of the whole matter would enlighten the country a great deal as to the way in which those agricultural philanthropists do business with their friends.

My hon. friend (Mr. Currie) is right in part when he states that the grain exchange was asking for an open market, but he is entirely wrong when he says that the farmers were asking for an open market a year ago.

I did not say that the farmers were, but hon. gentlemen opposite,
fMr. Maharg.]
who represent the Agrarian group and the Grain Growers, were yelling for an open market all the time.

The hon. member is
absolutely wrong. Hansard will prove, without any words of mine what attitude I took. I do not need to say a word; the hon. member can look at Hansard. Within three months after the board was first appointed, its continuance was asked for unanimously, without a complaint, at a shareholders' annual meeting of the largest elevator company in Western Canada, and that action was followed up right along to the day that the wheat board was discontinued. Every western organization, not only the associations, but the commercial companies as well, asked for the continuance of the wheat board. So that the the hon gentleman's statement that the farmers or those representing them wanted an open market, is absolutely wide of the mark, as everything published goes to prove that they were unanimously in favour of its continuance. Immediately they saw the personnel of the commission they said: That is the board we want; we want it continued just as long at least as there is controlled buying in the Old Country.

What does the hon.
member mean by "open trading"?
Trading on the exchange.
What did the sellers on the grain exchange want?

They did not want a
closed market at all; they wanted the gambling that has been going on. If my hon. friend has followed the workings of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange-
I do not follow gambling practices.

I did not say "if the hon. member followed the practices;" I said "if he followed the workings of the market." I do not think, for a moment, the hon. gentleman would indulge in practices such as that; but as a citizen of Canada and a consumer of flour, he should take an interest in knowing why the dealers charged practically as much for their flour when the mills bought their wheat at $1.50 or even as low as $1.25 a bushel as when they paid $4 a bushel for it. The difficulty in this country is that the consumers are not taking the interest they should take in the matter. A very pertinent question for the consumer to

ask is why they were charged the same price for flour when the wheat that it takes to make a barrel of flour was bought for $6 to $7, as they were charged when it cost possibly $20 for the same quantity of wheat. The hon. member should be interested in the matter as he is a consumer of flour, or he would not have the healthy appearance he has to-day.
The whole trouble with this open market is simply this. The man who headed the commission, Dr. Magill, came down here and preached and talked four-dollar wheat.
Five-dollar wheat.

Yes, four and five and six-dollar wheat. He quit this Government and was going to take charge of the grain exchange business in Winnipeg. Things were very rosy then. But six months before, the boys in the West had been using their grain certificates to light their pipes at poker games. A man would light a ten-dollar certificate at the candle thinking it was of no use whatever, and as a matter of fact tney turned out to be worth real money, something like bo cents, if I mistake not.
The difference between 15 cents and 63 cents.
They were very useful anyhow. I kept mine.

Somebody has made a tremendous loss. The Agrarian party have been pusyfooting this way and tnat. You never can tell where t,.ey stand on any question, and I think it is well to have an investigation to find out what was at the bottom of all this. When Dr. Magill was preaching five-dollar wheat, did any of the Agrarian party say, No, the whole world is buying-as nations, there is no individual buying? It was the nations that were buying the grain, just as they are to-day. Great Britain bought grain as a nation, so did France and all the other countries, so the only rational way was to trade in grain as a nation. No objection was raised to the open market. I did not see them parading any brass bands around or sending in any petitions against open marketing. Through the lack of common sense of the Agrarian group the farmers of this country lost $100,000,000, and we ought to have an investigation to find out what is at the bottom of it.

I would draw the attention of the committee to the
