fact that the item under consideration is the administration of the Canada Grain Act. I think the discussion that has taken place is not relevant to the item and I would ask hon. members to confine their remarks more closely to the item before us.

I would be quite prepared to do so, but the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) has made an accusation against the Agrarian group to which, in all fairness, I think I should be allowed to reply.
We had better adhere to the item under consideration at the present time. There will be other opportunities to reply.
Surely all this is connected with the grain ousiness. I think we should be allowed a little latitude in the matter. We have not been very troublesome in this corner.

I thought I had already alloweu very considerable latitude, but perhaps the committee will not object to the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) being allowed a reply; then we will return to the item under consideration.
The hon. member for Maple Creek has disclosed the fact that he desired a closed market in wheat for the purpose of increasing the price.
I must absolutely object to that statement. The hon. member is simply putting words into my mouth that I did not use.

I take it that that is the only logical deduction from the cry he made, because the market was not kept closed. He says the effect of opening it was to lower the price of wheat. At the same time he complains very much because the poor consumer has to pay so much for his flour. His argument is that the high price of wheat should be kept up for the Agrarians, so that the poor consumer can get flour at a lower cost. Such a proposition is absolutely ridiculous. It just shows the insincerity of the hon. gentleman, who is always clamouring in this House for free trade in implements and everything else, but who, when it comes to a question of his own bread basket, through wheat, says: Don't open the market; close it tight, so that we can make all the money we can, and by increasing the price of our wheat we will give the poor consumer cheaper bread. Did any one ever hear anything more ridiculous?

Facts cannot be disputed. My hon. friend will find that he has been paying for his flour lately just about what he paid when wheat was nearly three times the price it was at one time this grain season. My hon. friend from North Perth says that we asked for the open market in wheat. We never asked for any such thing. What we were talking of was trade on the exchanges in Canada.
Yes, but the hon. gentleman-
I must again ask hon. members to make their remarks relevant to the item under consideration.
I was going to speak to the resolution.

Order. The rule reads:
Speeches in Committee of the Whole must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
I think the committee quite realize that the discussion recently has not been strictly relevant to the item under consideration, and it is only for the purpose of expediting the business of the House that I now ask hon. members to confine their remarks to the item before us, which is the administration of the Grain Act.

We were discussing nothing but the operation of that Act. If we are to be limited to a discussion of what may happen in connection with this item in the coming year, the ruling of the Chair 
is all right, but I have never yet seen a Chairman in this House who was bold enough to close a discussion on what happened in connection with the item under consideration the previous year. It is the past year's operations we are discussing now, not what is going to be done in connection with this item this year. We are not projecting ourselves into the future, but endeavouring to discuss what happened in the past, which is of very great importance to this country.
Just one word in reply to the hon. member for Maple Creek. It is quite safe to say that if anybody hunts through Hansard he will find him on both sides of every question that ever comes up affecting the Agrarian party. You will find his leader on the one side, and perhaps my hon. friend on the other, just to ease up matters, so that if anything goes wrong, one of them will be able to say: We did not take that position. I challenge my hon. friend to show that his party or his leader took a decided stand against the open market. The reason they did not was that they were interested personally in having an open market. I say that a commission should be appointed to investigate and find the nigger in the woodpile.

I must take direct issue with the statement of my hon. friend that I have been on both sides of every question. I defy him to show by Hansard where at any time I have taken both sides of any one question. That I took one side while my leader took the other is not the question. The statement I originally rose to object to was that the Agrarian party had taken no action either in this House or outside when there was this talk of five-dollar wheat.

I do not agree with the hon. member for Maple Creek, and I do not believe that any one has ever said that that statement was not made on the other side. I think you could get quite a few in the Agrarian party throughout the west to agree with the member for Maple Creek, but my position is that that hon. gentleman does not speak for the Agrarian party. They have a chosen leader, and when the Prime Minister challenged him he did not say he was in favour of the wheat board. He said most unequivocally that he was strongly opposed to its continuance. Then what happened? That same hon. gentleman who has been chosen as leader in this House of the Agrarian party went to Manitoba and Saskatchewan, in both

of which places he was acclaimed the leader of the party. Within the last few months, since he made that statement in the House, he went to Saskatchewan and was chosen as their leader, and then he went to Alberta where he was also welcomed by that party and where his policy was endorsed. He is the leader of the party and speaks for it, and in that capacity he declared he was strongly opposed to the continuance of the wheat board. The hon. member cannot deny it, and I refuse him the right to speak for the party until he is chosen by them to express their views.

To be
fair, the hon- member for Regina (Mr. Cowan), should quote what my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) said.
I will get Hansard in a moment.	-

Keep
quiet; you have not the floor all the time.
It is up to hon. gentlemen to prove the position they take.
Order.
The hon. member for Marquette said that he did not want the wheat board continued as a permanent thing.

That is the point.
Mr- THOMSON: He never said that he was opposed to the continuance of it at that particular time; he was opposed to it as a permanent policy. Now, let the hon. member for Regina be fair or pretty nearly fair; at least, let him be as fair as he can.
When an hon. member rises in his place and challenges a statement it is up to him to produce Hansard.
Nothing of the kind.

I want to help the minister with his Estimates, but I think they are being obstructed badly at present by his own followers, who are straying quite a distance in the debate on this point. With regard to the attempt to expose the woebegone condition of opinion in the small Progressive group, I think my hon. friends are raising a tremendous tempest in a very little teapot. Why, Sir, it is one of the glories of this group that there is some independence of thought in it. In the last divisions in this House we have been the only group to show that it has capacity to divide on great issues
of public importance. We never see that quality on the part of my hon. friend from Regina, nor is it often displayed by the member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie)- However, let that go by the board. With regard to the position of the wheat board, I take it that we can all get our thoughts into a very narrow and satisfactory compass. I venture to think that there is not a single gentleman in this House who believes that the wheat board was to be a permanent institution in this country. I venture to assert that, and I do not observe anyone rise to say he considered that it should be permanent. It was an immediately post-war arrangement. There were differences of opinion amongst all thoughtful men as to the exact time at which the wheat board's operations should be suspended. There were differences of opinion in this group. My own view about the wheat board is that it is impossible to prove exactly that it was ever of any use to the western farmers. That is my own individual view. During the war anyone could sell at a high price wheat or anything else which the Allies wanted. I make that statement in support of my previous assertion. The same possibility of a difference of opinion arises in regard to the effect of the suspension of the board. Everyone knows that agricultural prices were bound to descend within a reasonable time after the close of the war. During the war, on my own farm in the West, we never took less than 50 cents a dozen for eggs; within the last few months-greatly to the benefit of consumers in this country, I hope,-eggs have gone down to 20 cents a dozen, that is all we are getting now. I suppose the operations of the wheat board have nothing to do with eggs at twenty cents.

Thirty cents.
_ Mr. CLARK (Red Deer) : My hon. friend is probably informed in regard to Ontario. His information on agricultural matters is no doubt wide, but he cannot correct me in any statement as to what the people in my part of the country are getting for eggs. I congratulate him that he is getting ten cents more. Now, as to my hon. friend's (Mr. Crerar's) position with regard to the wheat board, I am not at all sure that he ever made a definite statement. As I say, there were great differences of opinion as to whether or not it should be continued for another year. The Government was in great difficulties. I for one never attempted to increase those diffi-

culties because I sympathized with them, as I did in all reasonable cases where those difficulties arose from the prosecution of the war. Why is my hon. friend from North Simcoe trying to mix up the question of free trade and free exchanges with the wheat board and differences of opinion on that subject? Where does he want to get to? What is he proving? I submit that all he is doing is retarding the Estimates of the minister, and I do think we had better help my right hon. friend along.

The member for
Regina (Mr. Crerar) made a definite statement that the leader of this group had opposed the reappointment of the Canada Wheat Board. Now, in my speech on the address, I quoted from the speech of the leader of this party the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), in regard to this enabling legislation as introduced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, when this subject was before the House last session, and I shall read that extract. The original statement of the hon. member for Marquette may be found at page 4119, volume 5 of Hansard of last session:
Everyone who knows anything of the European situation must realize that conditions there are very unstable, and in those circum-sicnces I think, perhaps, there is Justification for the Government assuming the power which tney are asking for under this legislation.
That is a direct contradiction to the charge made by the member for Regina. Regarding the stand taken on this matter by the hon. member for Marquette, hon. T. A. Crerar.

What I said was that the hon. member was on both sides of the question. His whole speech was for open markets, but he concluded by saying at the end that on the whole the board might be continued for a time.

This discussion has demonstrated the difficulties that arise from the application of a vicious principle. To my mind the motive that prompted the institution of the wheat board was both vicious in principle and unjust in application. As the hon. member for Red Deer has said, I doubt very much whether it was of any use to the farmers. But we must admit that it was established at the instance of at least some sections of the agrarian community.
No.

It was surely not the eastern provinces that insisted on the institution

of the wheat board. Why is it vicious? It is vicious because by it the state instead of private enterprise undertook the marketing of wheat crops.
Does my hon. friend not recognize that in war the state must be the chief actor in a great many fields of activity, a role which it would not play in time of peace.

No. Not as generally as the hon. gentleman has just said, and not in this particular instance because my hon. friend has just shown that there was such a demand for wheat that time that there was no difficulty in marketing the western crop.

How then do you explain this fact: On the average we in Canada sold our wheat at a lower price than the Americans sold theirs. But during the operation of the wheat board the Americans operated on the open market and we under the wheat board, and got more money for our wheat than our neighbours across the line got for theirs.
It does not matter at all; it has no relation whatever to the principle I am now discussing.
It has, absolutely.

The fact that it had or had not that effect has nothing to do with the principle which underlies this question. All sections of the farming interest in Canada might have asked the Government for some assistance-the farmers of the province of Quebec, or the farmers of the province of Ontario, who grow potatoes, or hay, or any other kind of farm produce, could have come to the Government and said "organize a hay board, organize a potato board, so that when the crop is collected we may go to some government warehouse, or elevator, get a certificate and ask the government to finance our whole crop." Such a system is unjust, it is vicious, and it placed on the whole community a risk which the community should never have accepted. The wheat board fixed a minimum price of $2.15 for the wheat crop of the western fields. It is true that at that time $2.15 was quite a safe margin. But we were not under normal conditions, and it was possible for the wisest man to make an error in judging what would be the market price for wheat four or five months afterwards. Then having fixed $2.15 as a minimum price to

be paid the grain growers for their wheat the whole community would have had to stand a loss if the market price had fallen to $1.75, or some other lower figure. I say, this is a vicious principle; and the whole difficulty into which the Government was plunged in judging whether the wheat board should be continued or discontinued, arose from the application of that principle. It shows that a vicious principle should never be introduced into legislation to help in the solving of an immediate difficulty, because it always creates a greater difficulty and it at least creates a wrong precedent. Neither in the case in question nor in any other case should vicious principles be adopted in our legislation.

I was challenged by hon. gentlemen opposite to quote from Hansard anything which would show that the leader of the Agrarian party was opposed to the establishment or the continuance of the wheat board last year, and to its continuation as a permanent policy. This subject was under discussion for a considerable period last session. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) who was then leading the Government, correctly appreciated the situation. He saw that the Agrarian party were not taking a very definite stand on this matter and he challenged them to do so in these words:
I did not say I was closing the debate. I earnestly hope I have prodded these hon. gentlemen opposite-
That is the Agrarian party, sitting opposite-
- tc speak their minds. I was very much afraid tiiat the debate was going to close without a word from them.
Following that the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) took the floor, and during his speech he used the words which the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) has quoted to-day. But I wish to draw attention to the very unfair method followed by that hon. gentleman. The hon. member gave a quotation from his leader's speech, but he neglected to cite the qualifying language he employed and which I now propose to read. The hon. member for Marquette, the leader of tfhe Agrarian party said:
I think the Minister of the Interior furnished the only argument that constitutes a real reason why the board should be continued for another year, and that is the possibility of unified buying again in Europe.
These are the qualifying words which my hon. friend from Last Mountain did not read:
At the present time that is not the case.
Now the hon. gentleman (Mr. Crerar) meant that if there was unified buying in Europe he would continue the board for this year. At present there is not unified buying and therefore what is the only conclusion you can draw from the hon. gentleman's statement? It is that he was opposed to the continuance of the wheat board for last year. Having taken that attitude very definitely with respect to one year what does the leader of the Agrarian party say with respect to the Board's continuance as a permanent policy:
Personally I am opposed entirely to any permanent policy that meants the control of the marketing of grain in this country.
Could you have anything more definite than that? "There is no unified buying in Europe for this year consequently we do not need the wheat board and as a permanent policy I am opposed to it." There is no equivocation about that, it is straight opposition from beginning to end, and the hon. member was quite unfair in refraining from reading the expressions of opinion on the part of the hon. member for Marquette which I have just quoted.

This question has again come to the front owing to members on the Government side endeavouring to fasten the responsibility, upon the Agrarian group in connection with this matter. Despite all their efforts I do not think they have succeeded in converting the majority of members of this House to their belief; neither have they persuaded the people throughout the country that they are right, and after all they are the persons that are most interested. When this question was last under consideration a certain hon. member refused to answer a question that I put to him and the incident thereupon closed. However the subject has once more come to the surface, and perhaps it is well now to thoroughly ventilate the matter. But why, may I ask, do hon. gentlemen opposite endeavour to place the responsibility upon the Agrarian group, because we are not the dominating party in this House?
At whose request was the wheat board instituted?
I believe that the Government and their supporters were responsible.
But at whose request did they act?	.

Not at mine, for I was not in the House. However the point is, hon. gentlemen opposite were so wise they persuaded the Government that this was good legislation. They were able to forecast events so accurately they knew it was going to be a success. Being convinced of the likelihood of its successful operation they urged the Government to continue the operation of the hoard. At that time public opinion in the country was favourable to the continuation of the wheat hoard. Yet hon. members opposite are endeavouring to saddle members of the small Agrarian group with the responsibility of their action. Their conduct demonstrates that at one time they were shivering with indecision and they were not then so sure of their ground as they now appear to be, and they are indulging in all sorts of insinuations with respect to us which will not do us the least bit of harm. We try to reflect public opinion. I have done so since I became a member of this House. Speaking directly at the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders) who made the assertion that wheat in the United States sold for a less price than our wheat sold for under the wheat board, you might, Sir, remember this fact, that in United States by far the greater proportion of the total crop is soft wheat and should not equal our hard wheat in price. Therefore it is not fair to draw a comparison in that way. I can tell the hon. gentleman from personal knowledge that the hard wheats of North Dakota and Minnesota sold for a higher price than our wheat realized under the wheat board, and I have figures to substantiate my statement. Further than that, the assertion that was made-
I beg to state-
Order, order.

I am just answering the
assertion made that I was diametrically opposed to the wheat board. I want to say that if I lived close to the international boundary, and an open market obtained under the same conditions as prevailed in the fall of 1919, and if I had an opportunity to take my wheat across the international boundary, I would still take my chance of selling my wheat as an individual; but in the interests of wheat growers in the large areas far removed from the international boundary I would support the continuance of the wheat hoard. But I do know, as I

said in my speech on the Address, in the first speech I made in this House, that the individual who went across the line and accepted the Americans' money got thirty cents, seventy cents and as high as a dollar more than was received by the farmer who lived north of the imaginary line along the forty-ninth parallel of latitude. From this would be deducted the value of the participation certificate-48 cents a bushel.
The fact that the wheat board was not reconstituted last year, with the resultant loss of $100,000,000 to western farmers, which I think is very close to the mark, is the very reason why manufacturing establishments in Eastern Canada are closed to-day. The people who require the implements manufactured in those establishments have not got the money they expected to have from their crops, and consequently they are not purchasing. Conditions were upset by the action of the Government in allowing the wheat board to pass out of existence. Why are factories in Eastern Canada full of implements and obliged to shut down? It is because the people have not got the money with which to buy those implements, which were manufactured in anticipation that the purchasing public would require them.
I would like to ask the minister a question about the personnel of the proposed commission of inquiry into the grain business. Assuming such a commission is to be appointed, will the names be submitted to the House before the commissioners are actually appointed?

Order. I must call attention again to the fact that the matter under discussion is not the appointment of a commission to investigate the grain business, but an item regarding the administration of the Canada Grain Act. It is quite out of order on this item to, discuss the appointment of any proposed commission of inquiry.

Mr. Chairman, with all
deference I would say that this commission would have to enquire whether the Canada Grain Act had been wrongly ad-
5 p.m. ministered. I therefore wish to ask, in case such a commission of inquiry he appointed would the names of the proposed commissioners be given to the members of the House before they are actually appointed, so that we may have an opportunity to discuss the merits or demerits of the proposed appointees?
Now, Mr. Chairman-

May I have an answer
from the minister?

The hon. minister cannot answer that question because the matter involved is not before the committee. This is not our fight, it was started by the hon. member from Maple Creek, and we do not want to retire from the field without having the subject very thoroughly threshed out.
Finish the fight.

The most pithy saying
in the debate last year on this question was the statement of the leader of the Grain Growers' party, which has been quoted already, and I will quote it again. He said:
I think the Minister of the Interior furnished the only argument that constitutes a real reason why the Board should be continued for another year, and that is, the possibility of unified buying again in Europe.
Then he deliberately misleads the House in order to make his point-
Order, order.
He said-
Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. I submit that my hon. friend is out of order in charging any hon. member with deliberately misleading the House.
I said that he was misleading the country.
I say further, Sir, that my hon. friend is the only gentleman who would prefer such a charge, even if it were in order, against the hon. member for Marquette in his absence.

Yes, I am very sorry
the hon. member for Marquette is not here to take his gruel. But I did not say he deliberately misled the House-
Mr. Chairman, I must ask for your ruling on the point of order. My hon. friend charged the hon. member for Marquette with deliberately misleading the House.

I said he deliberately
misled the country, not the House.

No, you said
the House.

If the
hon. member did not charge the hon. member for Marquette with misleading the House, he is in order; otherwise he is not.

Then I will withdraw
the remark and say that he deliberately
misled the country, because he made a statement that there was no unified buying in Europe. As a matter of fact, unified buying in Europe continues to-day. Greece within the last week has bought four million or five million bushels of wheat in the United States. Great Britain has purchased all her wheat as a nation since the war and is doing so to-day. Lord Lee bought 180,000,000 bushels of wheat in the States last June. Why did he not buy here? Because we had no grain board to arrange credits with him for the purchase of such a large amount of grain. I say that by taking the deliberate action which they did the Agrarian group enabled the western grain speculators to sell wheat short in Chicago at from $2.80 to $3.00 a bushel, and then to kick the props from under the markets in the West and fill their orders with Canadian grain at $1.50. That touched the pockets of the farmers in the West, not the pockets of the grain operators or speculators there. Knowing as they did that the requirements of the British market were filled, and there would be no buying for six months or a year, they were the only people in the market and they put the wheat price down to the point I have stated, and their action cost the country about one hundred million dollars -perhaps I should not say it cost this country quite that amount, because I think some of these gentlemen got away with a lot of that money. I think we should have a commission to investigate who was at the bottom of selling out the western farmer and the eastern farmer. It has caused a lot of trouble to our agriculturists, and the gentlemen opposite very well know that they are being held responsible for the low prices by the farmers in the West.
"Angularly opposite."

Yes. The hon. member for Brome, of course, did not put himself on record on this question. But the leader of the Agrarian group, I say, misled the country in that statement-whether he misled this House or not-when he said that there was no unified buying in Europe. There was unified buying in Europe. He said he was in favour of a wheat board if there was unified buying in Europe, and then he said there was not unified buying, therefore the inference is that he wanted an open market. There was unified buying in Europe at that time, and there is to-day. Somebody has been misled and we must place the onus where it belongs. Hon. gentlemen "angularly opposite" expressed

great perturbation at the suggestion that this commission of investigation should be appointed. I hope that the Government will have the courage to appoint it and find out who has been digging into the markets out there, 'who has been selling short, who has been getting the difference betweeen. the $8 and the $1.50 which the Western farmer got. I do not hesitate to say that if the wheat board had been in existence last June the whole Canadian crop could have been sold by the board at $3 a bushel. The attitude taken by the representatives, so-called, of the Western Agrarians, has cost the farmers of the West $100,000,000, and that will require a lot of explanation on the part of my hon. friends when they go to their constituencies in the West.
I do not want to prolong this discussion; certainly I do not want to take up the extremely rash and unfounded statement of my hon. friend.
Now, I want a ruling, Mr. Chairman, because I have read the facts from Hansard, and I think I understand the English language as well as my hon. friend.
My hon. friend cannot prove, nobody else can prove, that $100,000,000 has been lost to the farmers of the West. It passes human proof; it is purely a matter of opinion on the part of my hon. friend.
The hon. member to your right (Mr. Maharg) said so to-day.

My hon. friend must open his ears, and to do that he needs sometimes to close his month. It is not usual in this House for two gentleman to talk at the same time. I want to point out to him that I listened with the utmost patience to what he said. I say now that neither he nor any person else can prove that the farmers lost $100,000,000 or any money at all by the dropping of the wheat board. I have given reasons for having believed that the prices of all agricultural products would drop within two years after the conclusion of the war. I, myself knew they would, because I have informed myself reasonably about the history of other wars and what happened when they were over. If I may be so personal, I may tell my hon. friend that in my little business on a farm in the West, which consists largely in the handling of cattle, I handled my cattle accordingly and sold them down

very largely, knowing that the high prices of the war would not continue. I have previously given my hon. friend the instance of the drop in eggs; I could do it in regard to butter. It happens in regard to every kind of agricultural produce and in my opinion it was sure to happen in regard to wheat whether you had the wheat'board or not. That is my opinion; my hon. friend holds a different view. I can tell him why agricultural produce falls, if he would like to know, and why it falls faster than manufactured goods do. Agricultural products cannot fall back upon the artificial aid of a tariff. That is why the farmers are the first hit. Yet I had to give $10 this morning for a pair of boots of a kind which I could have bought for $6 even after the war started. And so all along the line. I repeat that my hon. friend cannot prove-it is a matter of opinion-that the farmers of the West have lost $100,000,000. If they have, I want to say that there was nothing in the very careful and statesmanlike utterances of the hon. member from Marquette, which my hon. friend has read, to indicate that his attitude contributed in any degree to that loss. The Minister of Trade and Commerce will agree with me that the last and final responsibility for dropping the board for one year or carrying it on for another year rested with the Government of the day. The board was not suspended while Parliament was sitting; if my recollection is right, it was suspended after Parliament had prorogued. It was done by the Act of the Government. Now, it is not I, it is one of the followers of the Government, who says that the suspension of the board has cost the farmers of the West $100,000,000. If that be so, let him settle his charge with the minister whose Estimates are under discussion, who represents the Government for the moment; because he ought to realize by this time that his charge is directed, and directed solely, against the Government of the day. But if I could have proof of what my hon. friend believes so easily without proof, I certainly think he would have added an important reason for looking carefully into the votes that may arise during this session as to the advisability of keeping this Government in power a moment longer. Every question that comes up for a vote would be influenced mightily by a consideration such as my hon. friend has raised. I did not raise it; my hon. friend raised it. But I do want to

clear my hon. leader's reputation, if it needed it. His statements were of the most careful kind. And I want to tell my hon. friend something more: the wheat hoard has no existence in the political platform of the Dominion Council of Agriculture, the tariff platform which is the platform of this party. My hon. friend expresses great anxiety about how my hon. leader will clear himself with the farmers of the West when an election comes on. Well now, I really think there are parts of this House where there is more anxiety about what is going to happen when an election takes place than there is in the bosom of my leader. But in case my hon. friend is really and sincerely exercised about the chances of my hon. friend from Marquette in an election, let me assure him that he will be able to take care of himself among the farmers of the West, so far as I know anything about it.

Now, Mr. Chairman, we have heard the ipse dixit of the hon. gentleman; we all have to take our little licking from him. But he must have been asleep during the early part of this discussion, otherwise he would have heard the hon.' member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg), sitting on his right, make the statement that the loss was $100,000,000. I am only repeating hearsay; I do not know for a fact whether it was $100,000,000 or not. I do say, though, that this House, and I among the members of this House, have looked largely to the hon. member for Marquette for light and leading on this grain question. It is a national question, and a very serious one. When he made the statement in this House last year that he believed in a board, in national selling, as it were, when there was unified or national buying, and that there was no national buying, the inference was that it was his opinion that the board should be dissolved. At the very time he made that statement he must have known that the facts were entirely different. You cannot play fast and loose with the people all the time. But my hon. friend's information was wrong; his lack of knowledge in respect to the very question upon which he should have been informed has led this country to a loss of fully $100,000,000, as has been expressed by one of his own followers. For that reason, and as there is some difference of opinion as to the way in which the grain board, with which he is connected, functions, and
as there are questions that need to be asked of the grain board, I say again that the Government would be well justified in appointing a commission to go into this whole question and to fix the responsibility for the great loss which the country has sustained. We want to know the facts. The farmers to-day are not getting a better deal than they were getting before. The facts of the matter are simply these. There is just a small group selling fish, and they are calling everybody else's fish no good. They are dealing only in a particular brand of politics, and in view of the disastrous agrarian policies of Townley in North Dakota, which are of a similar character, this should lead this country seriously to investigate matters and ascertain whether the policies of the group represented by hon. gentlemen opposite are the best policies for the country, or whether they are only preaching socialism in a mild form. I have quoted the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), and his statement cannot be denied; I took it from Hansard; I took his word for it, and I think the Government took his word for it, because we knew if anybody should be interested in the farmers' affairs, he should. When we took his advice, we found that he was misinformed or he misled somebody deliberately, and the results have been disastrous to the farmers, so that if anybody is to blame for those results, he and his followers must be blamed.

May I refer for a moment to an expression used by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie), that is, as to unified buying? Last year I supported the Government in its policy as to the grain board. I thought it was wise that the Government should have the power to go on or to quit as, in its judgment and upon its responsibility, it decided. I think that probably was the position of the hon. member for Marquette. Unified buying at that time by Europe meant this, that all the buying was done by England and that the proceeds were distributed amongst the various countries in the order of their requirements. But that had ceased at the time we were discussing this, and instead there was buying by each country separately. One of the problems before the Government was this, that it must decide whether that buying by separate countries was going to offer a field or area of competition as would still give us prices that would justify us in opening the market. Apparently it did not entirely do that. I am, however, in-

dined to deal charitably with the Government with regard to its decision on that matter; but nevertheless the form of the term as used by the hon. member for Sim-coe North entirely (misplaces the judgment used by< the hon. member for Marquette with regard to the system of buying, and I think the latter's opinion was clearly understood at the time, although it may since have been forgotten by the House and, of course, by the country.

A quotation has been given from Hansard of a speech delivered by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar). I see the quotation stops at a very convenient place to suit the purposes of the hon. gentleman who made it. Had he gone further, it would have knocked the foundation from his argument. I follow directly after what has been read:
While during the years of the war the Royal Commission on wheat supplies in London had the practical control of the buying of wheat, and other cereals for that matter, since the Armistice has been signed the various count tries in Europe have each organized its own government buying agency. At least, this is very largely the case ; some of the neutral countries are getting back to old conditions of trade. Every one who knows anything of the European situation must realize that conditions there are very unstable, and in these circumstances I think, perhaps, there is justification for the Government assuming the power which they are asking for under this legislation.
If you take that altogether, the action of the Government had not the opposition at least of the hon. member for Marquette; it had his support. More than that, I think I am right in saying that, when the matter came before the House, there was not a single vote in opposition to it, certainly not by the hon. member for Marquette. If he had been opposed to it, he would have so voted, because we know the hon. member for Marquette is not in the least afraid to say what he thinks-if all the rest of the House were just as ready to give expression to their opinions as he has been, whether that helps or hurts him, the House would be conducted in a different way from what it is. Let me repeat what was said by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark). At the time this House prorogued the power for which the Government had asked was in their hands; they had enabling legislation to do what was required. They decided themselves, with that enabling legislation before them. Almost as soon as they got rid of Parliament, they decided that they would not have anything to do .
with the wheat board, and on them the responsibility rests.
The hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Yien) stated that the organization of a board of control of any kind, or words to that effect, was a vicious principle.

May I take the liberty of correcting my hon. friend? I did not say the organization of a board of any kind; I said the organization of a wheat board under the provisions of the statute enacted for that purpose, as the statute reads.

I am quite prepared to accept the statement, but that does not affect the point that I wish to raise. The hon. member wished to know at whose instigation this was brought about, or words to that effect. The impression that his remarks would leave on the House is that the farmers themselves asked for control in the matter of the marketing of wheat. I believe that is a fair inference to draw from his remarks.
Yes.
The original control in the fixing of price for the marketing of Canada's wheat during the war was never asked for by the farmers at all.
Could the hon. member inform me who instigated the organization of the wheat board?

It is not the question of the wheat board I am touching now; it is the original action of the Government in taking control of the marketing of wheat, -the wheat board is an after-consideration. The original control that was taken was not asked for by the farmers at all at any time; in fact, the opposite was the case. The minister himself will remember very well that when the original action was taken he asked that representatives of the western farmers should meet him in conference in this city, and we did so. And he will also remember that I opposed this action very strenuously unless he was prepared to take similar action in regard to the necessities that enter into the production of the grain, that is, to take control of the price the farmer should pay for his implements of production, his labour and so on. If they were going to control the price he was to receive, it was only fair that they should, in a measure, control the price it would cost him to produce.

The minister will remember that was my attitude. The point is, the Government having taken control, having stepped in, having broken down the organization, credits and such like, and having established that control, we believed in all fairness, some method of control should be continued. We did not ask the Government to appoint the wheat board. Committees from this House waited on the Minister of Finance from time to time, and they did not state any definite opinion whatever, but they asked him to institute some measure of control over wheat. This was absolutely refused. The question of the wheat board, however, is' an after-consideration and only arose out of conditions that had been created by the Government stepping in and taking control in the first place. Just where the instigation came from I am not prepared to say, and I am not objecting to it at all, but I believe it came from the allied countries in order that they might get control of the distribution of wheat. In fact, the chairman of the wheat executive in London told me there were only two reasons for it, one being to get control of the wheat and the other to keep the price down.
What was the nature of Government control before the institution of the wheat board?

Government control previous to the institution of the wheat board was under the Board of Grain Supervisors. I have already referred to their turning in $350,000 to the Government as a surplus from their operations. That board was discontinued.
How did it exercise control?
They fixed the price- the price of $2.20 per bushel for the wheat produced by the farmers all over this country.
Was it illegal to ask any higher amount?
Yes. They had absolute control over everything in regard to the fixing of prices and the disposition and direction of the grain. They had practically the same control as the wheat board.
That was vicious too.

I am not going to say whether it was vicious or not, but I might say that we did not ask for it. It is a matter of opinion whether if was vicious
or not, but we are not considering that question at the present time.
I am glad to hear that the hon. gentleman was opposed to the wheat board.

No, the hon. gentleman cannot put those words into my mouth at all. I was opposed to original control of the wheat in any manner, shape or form. We did not ask for it in any shape whatever, but when the Government stepped in and took control, we believed that in all fairness they should continue when they had broken down the organization that had formerly been used, more particularly when control buying continues in the Old Country. I was pleased to hear the hon. member for North Simcoe state that there was still controlled buying in the Old Country, for his leader (Mr. Meighen) when he was speaking in Saskatoon, gave as a reason for discontinuing the wheat board, the absence of controlled buying in Great Britain. What the leader of the Agrarian party said was absolutely right. There was no unified buying; that requires two parties, and there were no two parties buying jointly. But there was controlled buying in Great Britain and the allied countries, and there is to-day, although there was no unified buying at the time our leader made that statement, nor is there to-day. It is controlled buying that is in existence to-day by the governments of the different countries. It is the hon. member for North Simcoe's leader who will have the explaining to do and not the leader of our group.
Do I understand the hon. member for Maple Creek to mean that it was his desire that the Government should have continued to advance credits to foreign countries to buy our wheat last year and this?
If any such inference could be drawn from my remarks, that was not what I intended. That thought never entered my mind.

The point that I intended to make has been brought out so well by the hon. member for Red Deer that I shall merely call the attention of the minister to it again. I refer to the loss by this country last year of $100,000,000 of money. That amounts to $12.50 per head of our population. That much was lost at one fell swoop by some one's blundering. The establishment of the wheat board and wheat control was a matter of

policy on the part of the Government. First the Government got control buying through an agency which the hon. member for Maple Creek mentioned, then they established the wheat board. Both institutions were created as a matter of policy on the part of the Government. Then, later on, as a matter of policy the Government discontinued the wheat board. They said: We have come to the stage where the wheat board should be abolished. That again is a matter of policy for which the Government is entirely responsible. I was surprised to see the disloyalty, if I may use the word, of the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) this afternoon. He always votes for this Government, always stands by them when it is to his political advantage to do so, but to-day he tells the Government: You lost the country $100,000,000 of cold cash last year.

The hon. gentleman is putting words into my mouth I did not use. and is drawing inferences from what 1 said which are not justified. I did not make any such statement, or even imply it What I said was that we took our light and leading from the Grain Growers group and that we were misled; that was all.

That is a most
humiliating confession to make, that this Government, with twenty ministers, and agents and sources of information all over the country, did not themselves know what was the proper thing to do, but took a sort of sidelight, a remark that was not very definite that was delivered by some private member of the House, because that is all the hon. member for Marquette was. My hon. friend from Simcoe says that he swallowed that advice hook, line, and sinker, as the saying is, and passed it on to the Government, and that childish simple-minded aggregation thereupon inaugurated a policy that lost this country $100,000,000. And the extraordinary thing is that the hon. member for North Simcoe now says in all solemnity that a commission must be appointed by this Government to investigate why the Government themselves blundered and bungled the affairs of this country to the extent of $100,000,000. He does not realize the full force and effect of what he says. If he is right and the Government has bungled to the extent of this immense amount of money, the Government must take the responsibility, and the appeal must be to Caesar, and not to any commission.

I again protest against the hon. member putting words into my mouth or drawing inferences that are not justified- I said it was time that we had a commission to investigate the Grain Growers Grain Company and similar groups that were very much interested in seeing that wheat fell from $3 to $1.50 per bushel. They are the people who should be investigated.
There is no such company to my knowledge as the Grain Growers' Grain Company.
I may have made a single mistake.
Lots of them.
They have changed their name so often. It is now the North West Trading Company? They have had about sixteen different names.
Almost as bad as the Conservative party.

The question of the name does not matter at the moment. My hon. friend from North Simcoe, in the course of his remarks said that we were very much concerned over the possible appointment of this commission. Now I made my position clear on that a few days ago when this matter came up in the House- I said that we would welcome an investigation, and that so far as our company was concerned we would render the commission every possible assistance. Our objection is to the possible personnel of the commission. If a commission is going to be appointed, we want one that can do something, and that will take a little more action than the present commission has done which has every authority to do what this proposed commission will likely be called upon to do, if appointed. We want a commission that will be entirely independent of any other commission now in existence; and, I repeat so far as we are concerned we will give them every possible assistance, and it may be considerable too, when the opportunity is afforded to disclose some of the things that have been going on.

It rather strikes me after careful observation that we have pretty well exhausted this line of argument, and I am going to suggest to the committee that we now turn our attention to the work that is before us and show our good intention, in the first place, by passing this item.
I should first like to inquire from what quarter came the request for the establishment of wheat control and the fixing of a maximum price for wheat?

That is a very important question and as my memory is not in the very best order at the present moment, perhaps my hon. friend will allow me to take it into consideration and to give him an answer some of these days.
Mr, VIEN: That is very vague. I am afraid that if we let the item pass, I shall not get the answer until the Greek calends. The minister has on many occasions given evidence of a very retentive memory, and if he would jog his mind a bit I think he could easily recollect how it happened that the Canadian Government stepped into the wheat marketing business and undertook the establishment of wheat control and a maximum price. He may desire to rush the voting of this item, but I think he might make an effort to recall this thing.

We are not
rushing much, are we?
How is the increase of $175,000 in salaries, due to the reclassification, going to affect the bonus paid these employees?
I do not quite understand my hon. friend.

I will try to make it clear even if it takes a minute or two. Last year and the year before we voted a bonus to civil servants to meet the high cost of living. It was then understood that when the reclassification came into effect this bonus would in all probability be discontinued. I see now that the reclassification calls for an extra expenditure of $175,000 in salaries in this branch of the administration. What will be the policy of the department regarding the bonus in view of this increase?

The reclassification, as my hon. friend knows, affected all departments, and the bonus likewise applies throughout the Civil Service. The statement has already been made that the Government purposes this year to reduce the bonus by 25 per cent, and that, of course, will apply to this as to other departments.

Item agreed to.
Maintenance of Terminal Elevators and necessary equipment, $10,000.

['The reclassification, as my hon. friend knows, affected all departments, and the bonus likewise applies throughout the Civil Service. The statement has already been made that the Government purposes this year to reduce the bonus by 25 per cent, and that, of course, will apply to this as to other departments.']
How is this money to be applied? Is it for the upkeep of elevators, for improvements in plant, and so forth?
This is a very small vote which we have taken from year to year to be applied to capital account, if, for instance, new machinery is to be added, such as drying or cleaning plant.

I want to ask another question regarding the previous item. I was about to ask it when the chairman declared the item carried. We made provision during the last session for a certain amount of surpluses at terminal elevators being taken. Has any action been taken by the Government in that respect and have any returns come in from those surpluses over and above the actual grain which the elevators were supposed to have taken in?
You refer to overages?
Yes.

The hon. member will recollect that Parliament passed, either last year or the year before, an amendment by which the elevators are allowed a certain percentage, the rest of it coming into the consolidated revenue fund. That has been carried out.

Why should these
surpluses go into the consolidated revenue? This money, as well as some $350,000 of a surplus in connection with the operations of the Board of Grain Supervisors, has gone into the consolidated revenue. Why should it not be applied to the administration of the Act? This is what we had in mind when we requested that the overages over a certain amount be taken. While I am speaking about overages, it might be interesting to the House to know that when we took the overages away from the houses, the Board of Grain Commissioners immediately turned round and gave them an additional increase in elevating charges, which practically recouped them for everything they had lost in the way of overages. Now, that is a very significant fact. That increase was opposed by farmers' companies, but in the face of that opposition, the grain commission granted a rise of one half cent a bushel, which, on the whole handling of grain, amounts to approximately the total amount of money the different elevator companies received from their overages in previous years.
Is my right hon. friend correct when he describes this as a vote on capital account? It is not capital account in the ordinary sense in which we use the word in the Estimates.

No. In the first place, the elevators were built by a vote of Parliament. A vote was made for construction of elevators; and, so far as new construction is concerned, the capital account has been brought almost to a close. But we have had a small vote each year to provide for additional machinery. After that, the operating expenses come out of revenue. The expenditure has been very small. In 1919-1920, it was only $895; in 1920-21, to January 31, it was about $6,000, owing to addition of new machinery.

The words "capital account" do not, in the Estimates, mean quite the same thing as they do in the sense in which the minister uses them. This is capital account as respects that particular transaction, but it is not chargeable to capital in the sense in which we use the word in the Estimates.
It is for the maintenance of necessary equipment.
The minister did not answer my direct question in regard to surplus overages. Has any money been collected from that source?
That question has reference to the vote we have just passed. I will look up the information and get it for my hon. friend before we are through with the Estimates.

Item agreed to.
Trade Commissioners and Commercial Agents, including salaries, travelling expenses, contingencies and other expenditure in connection therewith, $230,000.
['That question has reference to the vote we have just passed. I will look up the information and get it for my hon. friend before we are through with the Estimates.']

May I ask what new
Trade Commissioners have been appointed since last year and where they are located?

During the
current year G. E. Short was appointed to Rotterdam, Holland, and Mr. E. L. McCall to Rio Janeiro, Brazil. The latter is a new appointment. I think we have not heretofore had a Trade Commissioner in Brazil. These are the only new appointments that have been made during the current year.

Was there no trade
agent at Rotterdam before?

We had one at Rotterdam many years ago and afterwards at Antwerp. During the war there was no agent at either place, but the office was kept open with a clerk there in charge in order to answer enquiries and preserve continuity as it were. This is a new appointment to Holland, and Rotterdam is the headquarters of the trade commissioners.
Have these officials passed an examination by the Civil Service Commission?
Yes; the appointments are under the Civil Service Commission.
And do these men possess the necessary linguistic qualifications?

Yes, so far as we could get them. That is a necessary thing. We make it a point as far as we possibly can that appointees to certain countries while passing through their period of probation here shall acquire the language of the country to which they go. In this case Mr. Short does not possess a knowledge of the Dutch language, but has a fair knowledge of French. You cannot in all cases get that linguistic requirement, but in most cases we make it an absolute necessity. For instance our commissioner to Brazil is familiar with the Spanish language and is fairly conversant with Portuguese, in which languages he will make himself more proficient. Our trade commissioner in Japan is a master of the Japanese language. I should not, perhaps, say a master of it, but he was born in Japan, as it happens, and during his school days, and ever since, has studied the language and has a good colloquial grasp of it.
Is he a British citizen?
Yes.

Who is the commissioner
to the Fiji Islands?

We have not
appointed anybody there.
Yes, we have a commissioner of some kind in the Fiji Islands?
No, not a Canadian Trade Commissioner.

Is there not a
gentleman there by the name of Catellier?
As trade commissioner?

Yes. In the
Fiji Islands.
, Sir GEORGE FOSTER: No.
This gentleman was certainly appointed to the Fiji Islands in some commercial capacity. I would like to know if he speaks the language used there, whatever it may be?
The hon. member will have to accept my statement that we have not appointed a trade commissioner.

He may have been eaten
by the natives.
My hon. friend could go there with perfect safety; they stopped the practice of cannibalism some time ago.
This should not be a matter of jest at all, because Canada does a lot of business with the Fiji Islands. Orders from there are now coming in fast, and there is quite a large trade growing up.
What do we supply to the Fiji Islands?
General merchandise.
We get a considerable amount of sugar from the Fiji Islands.
I suppose we supply the natives with clothing?

Yes, they require some.	.
Mr.	THOMSON	(Qu'Appelle)	:	How
many trade agents are there altogether?

At the present time there are twenty-four trade commissioners.
Mr.	THOMSON	(Qu'Appelle):	How
many are there in the United States?

Not one.
Mr.	THOMSON	(Qu'Appelle)	:	How
does the hon. gentleman explain that	state
of affairs? When practically half of our trade is with the United States why have we not some one looking after our trade there ?

I made rather an extended explanation about this matter the other day, and I can refer my hon. friend to the statements appearing in Hansard. I may say, however, that the main reason is this: We have never adopted the policy of placing our trade commissioners
in the United States, the two countries lying so close to each other, and the knowledge by one or the other of markets or marketing conditions being so easy to obtain, and being so generally well distributed. Access to either country is possible in a few hours, and there is a vast amount of intercommunication between the two countries. Neither this Government, nor any of the Governments which preceded it, has ever thought that it was necessary to extend through the United States our trade commissionership propaganda, but we have placed trade commissioners in more distant fields, where in the course of time, we knew our foreign commerce would extend with the idea of affording information and providing facilities for such expansion. The trade commissionership policy of the country has been a progressive one. It commenced really from nothing, or, more properly speaking, began with very few commissioners and involved but very little expense. It takes money to carry on this work on an extensive scale. Development has been carried on progressively as it was thought the necessity arose, and as we could provide reasonable means for carrying out the work. There are people who take the other view, that it would be well for us to place trade commissioners in the United States. If we commenced that policy it would require a large number of commissioners to cover the whole territory, and then the matter of expense comes in. The first question is as to whether it is necessary, and then there is the question of cost. I may say that the subject is engaging the attention of myself and my department, and probably before the session is over I will have an opportunity of speaking further with reference to it.

Before the war they had a system in Germany and Austria under which men well-known in commercial life were appointed to act as a sort of advisory board to the ministry. Has the Minister of Trade and Commerce ever considered the question of similar action along those lines?	f

Yes, I myself have considered the matter as to whether it would be possible to have an honorary board of advisors from different parts of the country. There is something to be said for it, and there is something also to be said, probably, on the other side. In a way we are getting advise though we have no formal board. Our department is in communication with all the Boards of



Trade, and with all the important centres of industrial trade acitivity. We are getting constant advice, and we are trying to give information on the basis of that advice. If my hon. friend were to see the correspondence which passes in the course of a month in the department I think he would he surprised at its diversity and volume. We are in touch with every quarter of the Dominion through its prominent business men and business and industrial organizations. Outside of that we have an excellent publication, the Bulletin, which we send to no one who does not apply for it and feels that it is necessary and useful to him. Our circulation in that way has gradually grown until now we have a live bona fide circulation of between eight thousand and nine thousand. We get commendation from our business communities as to its usefulness. In many ways it is utilized in a manner that we had not thought of. For instance, many school teachers use the Bulletin for lessons in geography and commerce and make those lessons of live interest to their pupils. Generally the policy which has been adopted is that our trade commissioners must pass from one to two and a half years in the work of the department before they are sent out into the field, and that work familiarizes them with the kind of information which they should gather. After their training in the departmental office we have those student trade commissioners travel through the country to examine the various industries and report to us thereon, and so make themselves fully acquainted with what is being produced, the way in which it is produced and the cost of its production. In these ways we seek to give them a training to equip them for their work, and with a knowledge of the language of the country to which they are assigned, which is the case in most of our appointments, these trade commissioners are able to do very efficient work. In short, I think we have a really good class of men who are rendering valuable services to our manufacturing industries.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When- the committee rose at six o'clock we were considering the . Estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce. We had reached and debated item number 358, concerning trade commissioners. Shall this item now carry?

Item agreed to.
Development and extension of Canadian trade, including exhibits and publicity, negotiations of treaties, miscellaneous advertising and print-ting, or other expenditure in connection therewith, $100,000.

Does this item cover
foreign exhibitions?

No. Exhibitions are really under the Department of the Interior. In this are involved certain small exhibits in connection with our trade commissioners' offices as illustrating the products of Canada.
What are the principal items of the expenditure?

The principal items of expenditure are in connection with the Exhibits and Publicity Branch, the work of which I explained the other night. In the Exhibits Branch we have articles from different countries which are tabulated and priced for the information of any manufacturers in Canada who may feel that we could supply any of those particular articles. The work is in its initial stage, and we shall see in the course of a little while what good really comes from it. Some good results, however, have already been obtained, and we feel that it will be of benefit to the manufacturing industries in connection with the supplying to other countries of articles similar to those exhibited. The Publicity Branch handles the film operations, which are very interesting and are a very valuable development in connection with publicity. At the Bureau of Exhibits on Wellington and Bank streets we have an equipment for the taking of pictures, the development of the films and their distribution. The work done there can-

not be excelled, I think, by any of the establishments engaged in that kind of manufacture. Our purpose is to give to the outside world a picture of our productive capacity, our natural resources, and so on; and we make the film story interesting by weaving in bits of scenery expressive of our natural scenic resources. These films are being distributed through a large number of the countries with which we are dealing now and with which we hope to deal. One of our pictures, for instance, that which depicts the water powers of Canada, is a very valuable one and has been exhibited in Great Britain and in the United States with profit in the actual realization of a great deal of business. Our agricultural film depicts the work of the settler, his coming into the Northwest, building his shack, beginning his operations, tilling his field and reaping his harvest. Then the movement of the grain is shown from the field to the elevator, thence to the cars and to the point of shipment to foreign countries. This very interesting film is a type of the many that we produce. Films illustrating manufacturing processes and activities are shown, in connection with fishing, logging, the manufacture of pulp from pulp-wood, forestry work, and so on, and the legends include statistics with respect to the particular resources dealt with. For instance, if it is water-powers, the available water-power is stated, the horse-power already developed, the capabilities of further development, and so on. These films are being so distributed that the distribution really costs nothing, and in fact, has now begun to bring us in a revenue. When I was in Great Britain two years ago I arranged a contract with one of the most prominent film exhibitors there, Sir William F. Jury, and he was so well pleased with the original films that he is taking a new film from us almost every month He puts them through his regular circuit and a certain percentage of the proceeds comes to Canada. We have been doing work in the film line for other departments. We have done some work for the Canadian National Railways which they would otherwise have had done elsewhere; so in that way we try to keep our staff employed and to make as large as possible the income Which is set against everhead expenses. During the latter half of the last year we did work for the departments to the amount of $8,559. We have now a large list of these motion pictures which have been taken and distributed. The total of the revenue up to January 81, 1921, is $11,875.
93i
For the current year.

No, from the time they began distributing these pictures, probably about fourteen or fifteen months in all. In the United States these are distributed and are shown to probably two or three million people weekly, who see them through the pictures of current events. They also have been distributed in like manner in New Zealand, Australia and South Africa, and we are having the legends printed now in other languages so that they may be distributed in other countries as well- They were exhibited in France during the time of the Lyons Fair and at Paris when we had our exhibition there. This serves a double purpose. It stimulates trade; it excites curiosity as to our natural resources; but it also does a good deal of the best of work for our Immigration Department. It was a personal experience that I had at Paris and at the Lyons Fair. The city of Lyons set apart one of their large halls for the exhibition of our films, and we exhibited them there in the afternoons and in the evenings. The hall was crowded all the time, and it was very gratifying to see the interest that the people took in the pictures and to hear the remarks which they made in reference to them. The same thing occurred at Paris where we exhibited these pictures for about three months, where schools and colleges made expeditions at certain hours to see them, where the general public also came in, and where I had an opportunity of having them viewed by all the staffs and members of the countries represented at the Peace Conference, to whom I sent personal letters inviting them to come at certain times, so that we got a very wide publicity in that respect in reference to our resources and other features of interest.
What amount was expended last year on these pictures out of the appropriation of $130,000?
Up to January 31, about $86,000. We have reduced the appropriation $30,000 this year.
What amount was expended on account of negotiations of treaties, and was any amount expended in connection with the proposed treaty with the West Indies?

Out of this appropriation we paid the expenses which were incurred by the meeting here. We provided the hall without expense; we met in the museum, and we took care of the

delegates while they were here. With the co-operation of the Board of Trade and the citizens of Ottawa, we gave them as good a social time as we could. We also paid the small printing expenses.
What was the amount of the item?
I have not seen the bills that are in. A very small amount comparatively.

I notice from the right hon. gentleman's report that a preferential tariff has been extended by Australia to the United Kingdom and there is some little temporary agreement between Australia and South Africa giving South Africa a tariff preference also. The right hon. gentleman's report says that "the Canadian Government is now considering an exchange of views with the Australian authorities in the hope that the trade relations between the two countries may be improved." This report is dated 1st June, 1920. What has occurred in connection with these negotiations, and what success or failure have they had?

South Africa received a small preference in the Australian market on a very limited number of goods, and I think South Africa gave three or five per cent preference on a certain^ limited number of Australian goods. That is the only preference that Australia has given other than to the United Kingdom. In Australia they undertook, about two years ago now, a revision of the tariff. I am not going back beyond that because I suppose my hon. friend knows what took place before that. There have been negotiations for the extension of preference between the two countries, but they have never resulted in an actual preference being given in either case, there being several reasons for this. The Government which at present exists in Australia, when it came into power, undertook a revision of the tariff. In March, 1920, it brought down a resolution which was the basis upon which was to be founded a Bill and an Act, but the Bill itself has not yet been framed and passed by the legislature; only the resolution holds, and the Government is acting under the resolution. By that resolution Australia gave a preference to British goods, but gave no preference to any other outside dominion or dependency of Great Britain, but in the resolution she contemplated, after the legislation was completed, opening negotiations with Canada and New Zealand for preference be-

tween herself and those countries. As I have said, the Bill is still being discussed, and the latest advices that I have is that probably it will be autumn of this year before it is finally passed. Whilst I have been keeping in close touch, personally and otherwise, the answer has been invariably this: "When that Bill becomes law, we shall have our legislation, and we shall be very glad to take the matter up with you and see if we can arrange for a preference between these countries." In the meantime the present condition is that Australia made material additions to her tariff along protective lines, gave to Great Britain a fairly good preference on her products as Australia imported them, but has no other preferential arrangements either made or under negotiation. That is the situation as it is to-day, so that our manufactures going into Australia, if they are of a quality or kind like those that come from Great Britain, go in under the general tariff while the British goods go in on a basis of preference.
We do not give Australia a preference?
No, we have never been successful in getting an arrangement.
Suppose this Bill is passed by Australia, what do they propose doing as far as the Dominions are concerned? What reciprocal arrangements are suggested?

There are none suggested by the Australian Government. There is simply in the resolution I have spoken of power to enter into negotiations for a preference, but there is no proposition, and there are no negotiations. The answer I invariably get is that as soon as this Bill becomes law they will take the matter up with us.
The Bill will empower them to make any arrangements they please?
Yes.

We had a partial arrangement with Australia at one time. At the beginning of the preferential arrangement my recollection is that we extended the preference to New South Wales, which was at that time a low tariff colony, but we did not extend it to Victoria, which was not a low tariff colony. When the colonies were united in the Commonwealth of Australia, the tariff generally got a lift up, and from that time forward we did

not give a preference to any part of Australia. That is the present condition, I assume.

We are not
giving a preference to any of the states in Australia.

I quite understand
that, because when the colonies united and had a common tariff, that tariff being not as advantageous to Canada as the tariff of New South Wales had been, we ceased to give a preference to any of them.
Does my hon. friend refer to the first legislation of 1897?
Yes.

That was the legislation, if I remember rightly, under which Canada gave a preference to any country whose tariff came within a certain limit. That might have applied to New South Wales, but when the main preference came in, none was given to Australia.

Will any part of
this vote or any other item in the Estimates be used to promote trade within our own Dominion?

No, this vote is for the encouragement of foreign trade, but we cannot, I suppose, very well promote trade with outside countries without it having a reflex action on ours. This vote is not for any such purpose as my hon. friend has in mind. The different provinces interchange their goods, producers trade with consumers, and we do not by this vote, or any other vote in the way of subsidy or monetary encouragement, strive to aid that process of merchandising.

I understand that Mr. Hoover, who was Food Controller in the United States, is very anxious to develop trade within the borders of that country, and I was in hopes that our Department of Trade and Commerce might be able to do something along that line, especially with respect to fruit. I had in mind aid to our growers in finding a market for their fruit. There is a great demand for fruit, but thousands of barrels of apples and smaller fruits go to waste every year owing to the scarcity of labour and of containers. We are not able to get this fruit on the market in bulk form, and I had hoped that the department might aid in finding a ready market for these perishable fruits. I think it would be a great
benefit to the consumers in all the large centres. The high-priced containers certainly mean a higher price for the fruit to the consumer, but if the department could co-operate so that this fruit could be shipped in bulk or in sacks it would reach the consumer at a much lower price. Owing to the scarcity of labour in the rural districts and especially in the fruit growing districts, aid of this sort would be of great benefit to the consumer.

The different
industries, the fruit industry, for example, are helped by the work of this department. The fruit industry i6 helped by the work of the department in gaining an entrance for it and in developing its distribution in foreign countries. It would be a wonderfully complex piece of business if we undertook here, in this Dominion, to aid the producers in any one section of the province to get their articles into another section or from one province into another province. That opens up a vista of a very [DOT] great deal of complexity and expense. I think for a considerable time, maybe always, our internal trade will have to look after itself in so far as the transportation and representation of its products is concerned in other parts of the Dominion. The Statistical Branch of my department is doing a great deal of valuable work towards making the people of this Dominion acquainted with what is produced in different sections, its quality, quantity, price, and the like of that. Those parts of the country which do not produce a particular kind of article get that information, and that in itself is quite a large measure of aid and stimulus towards internal marketing. There is nothing in this item for the purpose my hon. friend speaks of, nor do I think anything will be voted along that line.

I was lead to bring this matter up by a speech I read of the Minister of Finance delivered to the Retail Merchants' Association, from which I will quote only a short extract:
Canada's chief claim to prosperity is as an agricultural country. There is no doubt of that. Does it look well for an agricultural country to be buying its agricultural products from abroad? Are we city people fair to our farmer ' cousins? Are we trying to see the home market retained for our own farmers as we should? Does it not seem strange that in a country like this, with such a climate, that for the nine months ending December 21 last we imported if27,000,000 worth of fruits, fresh and canned,

from the United States? What is the matter with the Canadian apple? Obviously something must be wrong somewhere.
