During the nine month period referred to we imported 198,000 barrels, three boxes to the barrel, with our own apples rotting by the thousand on the ground. Whatever it is which is wrong must be mended.
Having read that, and having had some experience in this matter, I felt that there was a great and needless waste of fruit in Ontario when there should be a ready market in our large centres and in the West; for we all know the food value of the apple. Now, we made an attempt last fall to ship apples through to Winnipeg in bulk and not in any container, and we discovered that this could be quite successfully done, although I think there is room for great improvement. We understand that in the Niagara district a large corporation has been formed and the Ontario Government has guaranteed the salary of an officer for the coming year to supervise the work that is to be carried on. If we could secure real co-operation on the part of the Department of Trade and Commerce in the way of advertising and so on, not only the producers generally, but the consumers in the large centres, would be greatly benefited. The consumers are very desirous of getting this fruit as cheaply as possible, and we are equally anxious to dispose of it at reasonable prices. So that the co-operation of the department along this line would, no doubt, meet with the approval of both consumers and producers.

I think my hon. friend has about struck the point in the last sentence or two. If there is one section of the community that has a large product which it wants to get rid of, and there is another community somewhere at a distance that has both the capacity and the desire for this product, then there is room and there is need for co-operative effort. Some organization is obviously required to bring supply and demand together. But my hon. friend must remember that some of the departments are doing a good deal in this direction. For instance, take the Department of Agriculture, among the different branches of which is the fruit department. If my hon. friend will study its reports, or listen to its minister, he will find out that the department is doing a great deal to promote the consumption of fruit and other products. And the Marine Department has also done something to encourage the consumption of fish by establishing a fish day. After they have succeeded in firmly establishing the habit of observing one fish day, 
I suppose a second such day will follow. By this means, the consumption of fish ought to be greatly increased. Some years ago I put on a campaign to aid the-fruit industry, advising everyone to eat an apple every morning. A very successful advertising scheme was carried out and a great many apples were eaten that would otherwise have been wasted. That, however, was not a settled policy. After all, the industry itself must look out for its own avenues for customers and transport, and under this vote my department does not in any way contribute to that business.

I may give the
minister a concrete example of the cost to the consumer and it will show that something is needed. Perhaps I am appealing to the wrong department, but if the Department of Agriculture is properly charged with the responsibility for a matter of this, kind, I trust it will give it some attention. We loaded cars on the Canadian Pacific railway last fall with bulk apples, hand picked, at $1.30 per hundred. The freight on these apples into Winnipeg amounted to $1 per hundred, which meant a cost of $2.30 per hundred landed there. These same apples were then retailed at $1.85 per fourty-pound sack, and the people came and bought them, at the car, paying something like $4,621 per hundred. Someone was thus making a profit of about $2.30, which seems to me to be too much of a spread if business is to be successfully carried on. Now, we feel that if we could be put into closer touch with the consumer, it would benefit us both. 1 am sorry if I am appealing to the wrong department; but, I repeat, I hope something will be done, either through an advertising campaign or by some other effective means, to secure closer co-operation and communication between consumer and producer.
We export lai'ge quantities of butter and cheese every year to the United States and Great Britain. What is the department doing to extend this trade?

My hon. friend sets me a pretty large task if I am to tell him all that the department has done in the interest of trade. I do not think he quite means that I should give a lecture that would occupy the time which it would take for me to recount the operations of the department. As regards butter and cheese, neither of these is a product which has come to light within the last few days, or even within the last few years. The cheese industry of Canada established its

reputation in Great Britain decades ago, and it does not require anything in particular more than to keep up the standard. If possible, we should strive to improve the quality of our butter and cheese, and everything advisable in this respect is being done by the Department of Agriculture which looks after our butter and cheese and the dairying business to ensure that quality is maintained. If that is done, the market having been once opened, the demand created, the taste for these articles cultivated, and their reputation thoroughly established, trade must do the rest. My hon. friend, of course, does not think that we can go further than that. We cannot transport these products or open warehouses for their sale; that does not come within the scope of the department's activities. But we have, by the collection and distribution of information, done all we can to further the industry. The same applies to other articles.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, in taking my seat this evening, I promised the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce that I would furnish my humble contribution to the evening's debate by making a few remarks in French.
We know and it gives us much pleasure to acknowledge it, that he is about the only scholar within the Cabinet and that he alone together with one of his colleagues, the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), may pay themselves the compliment of knowing and speaking French. We congratulate him. I wish to prove to him this evening that we appreciate his work, by taking up an industry that interests the whole country. Every year we export about $50,000,000 worth of butter, cheese, condensed milk and cream. In reading over the official statements which are placed at our disposal, the right hon. Minister will no doubt recall to his memory that we export to England at the very most between $10,000,000 and $12,000,000 annuah-ly of butter and cheese. According to the reports of the Department of Agriculture, we are one of the smallest exporters of butter and cheese to England. As a matter of fact, only France and Belgium, I believe, export less butter and cheese to England than we do. I can easily anticipate the right,hon. Minister's answer that it is up to the Department of Agriculture to look after that end; but on the other hand, what benefit do we derive from the Ministry of Trade and Commerce, if all the other departments not only take care of the production but also attend to the foreign marketing of their respective products. Such being the case, there would be no need for a Deparment of Trade and Commerce. This is perhaps a truth known to everybody, yet no one dares utter it in public.
I am perfectly of the opinion of the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, when he tells us that the Department of Agriculture sees to the production of butter and cheese. I know that the hon. Minister of Agriculture personally gives to it much of his valuable time and energy. In order to ascertain the quality of his products each year in either one or another of the provinces of this country, he organizes fairs at which all the provinces are invited to exhibit their choicest products. Last year, or rather a little more than a year ago, one of those large exhibitions was held in Winnipeg, and Quebec carried olf a fifth prize. During the last session 1 had the honour to promise my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) that the next exhibition would show whether we had improved, and I think my memory serves me well when I state that this year, the large Dairy School of St. Hyacinthe took a first prize. We, then, have first-class products, but we cannot ask the Department of Agriculture who is looking after production and tries to keep up quality, to find new markets for the surplus of those products. In fact, if we look up the Estimates of the Department of Agriculture, we find that there is nothing to warrant an expenditure by that Department towards finding an outlet abroad for our surplus of products, whether in the United States, France or Great Britain.
But, is it not rather strange, and I think the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce should be the first to acknowledge it, that countries situated at the Antipodes got ahead of us on the English market, that the products of Argentina, New Zealand and Australia arrive there in larger quantities and that a better price obtains for them than for our Canadian products. I think it is within the purview of the right hon. minister to ascertain why countries so unfavourably situated should have this advantage, while our country, so near to England, and with such an extensive merchant marine, should have such small shipments to Great Britain. He should find out why we are unable to find in England a market for those commodities which are there in great demand and of which we have a considerable surplus. This is even more striking when considered in the light of the
1472.

situation of the dairy industry in Ireland. We are aware that since unrest has broken out in this most unhappy part of the empire more than thirty large dairies, creameries and cheese factories have been destroyed by fire. Moreover, the Department of Agriculture does not allow the exportation of butter and cheese from Ireland except at fixed prices. Again we know that the butter which was smuggled from Ireland into England sold at five or six pence above the price fixed on the English market.
Taking all these facts into consideration, I am of the opinion that our Department of Agriculture should take more interest in the exportation of our dairy products. Our dairy, creamery and cheese factory products do occupy a special position in the country.
The hon. member (Mr. McDermand), who a moment ago showed his interest in the production and sale of fruit in this country, was told by the hon. minister that the department did not supervise internal trade. In my opinion, the department should at least show some interest in our foreign trade in a commodity which is not the produce of a province exclusively, but of all the provinces. Every province in the Dominion is interested in seeing to it that its butter, cheese, cream and condensed milk command better prices and sell in larger quantities. The result of such an undertaking is obvious. The owners of those small factories transact their business directly with a large number of farmers and, in helping those small manufacturers-I think they may be called manufacturers just as well as those who have steel, iron, etc., as their raw material-I am sure the department would be carrying on some useful work. The butter or cheese manufacturer gets his raw material from the farmer and pays him in proportion to the returns from the sales. If we create a larger market for our butter and cheese, the effect will be felt at once by the farmer and the country at large. It is not only a section of the country but the whole Dominion that would benefit by it. What is the use of voting for the Department of Agriculture amounts aggregating about a million dollars, and even more, to promote the better breeding and better care of our herds of cattle, if after all this the Department of Trade and Commerce does not exert itself in order to find a market for our products. From the special statement made to-night by the hon. minister, one would think that the Department of Trade and Commerce is nothing but a film machine, a photographic screen. If the Government of this country

is going to do business with moving pictures as a specialty, there is but one thing to do: turn this House into a public hall and give us moving pictures concerning the intentions of the Government. We would have them before our eyes and the Government would not be committed in any way, as they would not have to say either yes or no. Moving pictures might help in making Canada better known to foreign countries; by their means, immigrants might be attracted here; but I do not believe that they would prove satisfactory to foreign dealers and induce them to purchase our products, though they might bring these dealers to invest money in our country, and perhaps come to see which industries could be developed here; yet, I fail to see how our trade could gain any advantage in this. All the reports of the weekly bulletin which is distributed to us-reports which unfortunately are published in one language only -prove that it is important that the Canadian dealer make some arrangement with the English dealer in regard to his sales, delivery and manner of payment, and also the packing of Canadian products. What do we find in pursuance of the advice given in this Bulletin which is published under the direction of my right hon. friend? We find moving pictures. They may. be very nice and most enjoyable to look at but they are of no help, or very little, to trade. The right hon. minister and his colleagues who accompanied him to the conference of the League of Nations, may have found the sight of our movies most enjoyable but, after all, these gentlemen ought to realize that there is something better than movies to be offered to foreign countries. Is the Government of Canada a moving picture firm? I think this is of a nature to have us turned into ridicule, and if all may spend a pleasant afternoon or. evening at a movie show, there is not much advantage there for our dealers.
We have companies and co-operative organizations in thq province of Quebec. We have the large co-operative society of cheese-factories of Quebec which comprise 8,000 members, and which carries on a trade of several million dollars in foreign countries; this is indeed the only large trade organization which is seeking a foreign market for our farm products, and particularly for butter and cheese manufactured in our province. I cannot say what is being done in other provinces, but I know that there -are large warehouses in these provinces, that there are dealers who are busy marketing a few million pounds

of Canadian butter in Great Britain. I think that the Argentine Republic shipped to England, last year, over 300,000 cwt. of butter, whilst Canada only shipped 32,000 cwt. at the most. Why this discrepancy? I cannot say, and would be glad if the hon. minister himself could suggest an explanation, though I doubt very much he will do so. Neither could it be explained by the movies. It would be most important, especially under present circumstances, that the minister should have under his orders, smart, active, pushing young men 'who understand business, and who could represent us and make our products known in England and the United States.	>
Nearly every day, on the floor of this House, we hear hon. members saing: "You must, we must do our best to trade with our Mother Country, with Great Britain." We would be delighted to sell our products to Great Britain. Only, we realize that our Department of Commerce is not adequately represented in England, that it is not represented in such a way as to help us. I believe that, under these conditions, a fifty million dollar trade should prove of greater attraction to the minister and induce him to take all necessary means so that this product-a product which is greatly needed by the British people, especially cheese which is as bread and wine to the British labourer, cheese which is his principal food -be delivered to him in as large quantities as possible by our country and not by the Argentine Republic or New Zealand or Australia.
I wish to tell the hon. minister that I believe that he, himself, together with the other members of the Government should see to the exportation of products which are manufactured by the farmer or by those who receive the raw product from the farmer. It is very well to attend to large industries; these are generally controlled by large business concerns, men of wealth, who can very well look after their own connections and interests on the European markets.
Until late years, we have had a representative in Europe soliciting orders from the allied countries for our different manufactured articles. This gentleman, though paid by the Dominion, has never very much exerted himself toward establishing commercial relations which might have helped in developing the trade both in the raw material and the manufactured article supplied by the Canadian farmers.
Why this discrimination, which is constantly recurring? Why trouble about the
large manufacturers and never about the agricultural class?
The fiscal year of 1919-20 shows us that about fifty per cent of the total exports of this country consists of products foreign to our large industries. For fifty per cent consisted of farm products, either in their raw state, or as manufactured goods; this being the case, why does not the Department of Trade and Commerce think it proper and expedient to bring on closer commercial relations with England which is our best market? Why do they not see that we export even more to the United States, which seems to be, at the present hour, the largest market in the world.
I hope that the hon. minister himself will deem it expedient to explain some of these flaws which exist in his department, and why he has erred, and if having erred, he wishes to find grace by creating at an early date, for the Canadian farmer, the manufacturer of butter, cheese, condensed milk or cream, a market worthy of our country. What benefit is derived, by the Minister of Agriculture, from stimulating agriculture and asking the farmers of this country to produce more and of a higher standard, if having done so and more than the population of this country can consume, his colleagues, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, cannot find the'necessary outlet for the sale of the surplus of these products.
I think the right hon. Minister of Commerce should stir up his head officers if necessary, and put them to work, so that we, the small as well as the large producers, may profit from the work of his department.

I would like to intervene at this stage in order to call attention to a subject which was discussed very briefly this afternoon and which discussion seemed to end in rather an indeterminate manner-that is the importance of considering how much we can do for Canadian trade by establishing commercial agents in the United States. As it is now, those in the adjoining Republic who want to buy Canadian goods have no way of determining the extent of a particular trade or the rates in vogue, and we are accordingly at the greatest disadvantage in that respect as compared with the United States. The latter country has seventy or eighty commercial agents in Canada, most of whom are consuls, and these officers are furnished with admirable trade statistics of the manufactures of their country, and are

able at any time to supply those who are in want of goods from the United States with details in regard to railway rates and other data. We have no service of the kind in the United States, and the consequence is that Canadian manufacturers and producers are at a very great disadvantage in obtaining or filling orders from there. We now know that we are buying from the United States double the amount we export to that country, and this handicap could be largely overcome-so I am told by those who know, and it seems to me quite obvious-by having a better system of advertising our goods in the United States and indicating where reliable information could be obtained as to Canadian industries or products. The expense of such a proceeding would not be great for this reason: I am told, upon reliable authority, that the commercial agents of the United States in Canada-who, as I said before, are consuls and have consular offices in all our large centres-are paid fees by Canadians on the commercial paper involved in sending goods to the United States, and that these fees in the aggregate are sufficient to pay the entire salary or remuneration enjoyed by these commercial agents. We have therefore the extraordinary state of affairs that Canadians are paying the salaries or remuneration received by American officials, but Canada is getting no advantage from the value of the goods exported. I was told of a case by a gentleman in New York who received an enquiry from a manufacturer in New Orleans desirous of obtaining maple sugar and syrup from Canada. Unfortunately he did not know where to go. There was no Canadian agent to whom he could apply, and New Orleans is hundreds of miles away from this country. In some way or other he finally got information, through some agent in Montreal, as to where he could obtain these commodities and the result was that an order came from New Orleans for maple sugar and syrup to the extent of two carloads valued at several thousand dollars. If such a profitable transaction resulted in this' one case, how many more instances are there where Canada loses orders for trade simply because of the fact that the people living over there, at such a distance from this country, have no information as to where to place their orders. If it is a fact that the salaries or remuneration which the American trade agents, or consuls, in this country receive, come from fees paid by Canadians, it seems to me that the same 
result would follow if Canadian trade agents were established in the United States. It would appear that if we could collect fees for Canadian trade agents appointed in the large American centres those fees would equal, and perhaps exceed, the remuneration that should be granted these officers, so there would be no extra expense to our country in putting such a system into effect. At present the work over there, as regards Canada, is done by the British consuls established in the large cities. While no fault can be found with the attention they give to Canadian affairs, they are not particularly anxious to see that Canadian orders are placed. They are British consuls, they are looking after the trade of Great Britain and Ireland, and while they are willing to do what is requisite there is no special effort made by them to help in the placing of Canadian orders. But if we had our own agents over there, and if a certain amount were placed at their disposal for the purpose of advertising in the papers where they were to be found, and what information they could give, I venture to say that a very large amount of the present disparity in the trade between the two countries would soon disappear, and we would find our Canadian business men deriving very great benefit by the appointment of these trade agents.

I would like to ask the minister, in connection with the item to cover the expense of negotiating treaties, whether the Government has in mind, or has attempted to negotiate, a treaty with England permitting live Canadian cattle to be imported into that country. We give a preference to British goods entering Canada, and I should think that if this Government displayed sufficient activity it could, in exchange for that preference, get permission to have our live cattle landed in Britain. The cattle industry of Canada is going to be very badly crippled if our livestock is excluded from the American market by a high tariff, and shut out entirely from the British market. I would not suggest that the minister should retaliate by increasing the duty on British goods, but I would recommend to him that if Britain is not agreeable to admitting our live cattle, we should reduce the customs duties on goods coming from other countries and make them equal to those prevailing on goods coming from Britain. Has the Government contemplated any such plan as the one I have suggested?

No, we have not thought of anything along that line, in order to achieve the object referred to, but my hon. friend knows very well the position which has been assumed by the Dominion for a great many years past with reference to this question. I think probably the matter will be in a better position by the Government continuing along the lines which have been followed in the past, and which are still being followed, rather than to interject into the issue a tariff question by way of reprisal. I do not think that would be the best way to reach a satisfactory conclusion.
With regard to the point raised by my hon. friend from Parkdale I may say, as I have already stated to-day, that my department is giving very special attention to the subject, and I repeat what I said this afternoon that probably before the end of the session I may have something further to say in a more definite way. The arguments which the hon. member has placed before the committee are believed in by a great many people; but there are others who think that trade between ourselves and the United States might very well be left to take care of itself for the reasons which I have already given. The two countries are in close proximity to one another; they have an intimate knowledge of each others resources, and in a variety of ways they are largely informed as to the extent of the business which each country may do with the other. Then the cost must be taken into account. For us to adopt the consular system which the United States employs and apply it to the United States would necessitate a rather heavy expenditure. The United States' consuls in this country number not more than thirty, and they are supplemented by a certain number of agents. It is true that for every package which is invoiced a fee of $2.50 is charged, and those fees in the gross more than cover the salaries and emoluments of these consular officers and their agents. If we adopt that system we must be prepared, as I said, to apply it to all foreign trade; otherwise it would be considered discriminatory against the United States. Of course, it would not be necessary to apply the system to Empire trade. As I said before, the matter is being considered.

I would like the privilege of going back, as did the hon. member
for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) to the item preceding, which varies very much from the present item. I am inclined to say a few words in advocacy of the same principle suggested by him. From what the minister-said the other night, apparently he is thoroughly satisfied with his trade commissioners whom he has at work in various foreign countries, but I do not think he has yet given to the House the names and locations of those gentlemen. I should like to see this information put on record as a matter of publicity so that we may know who those gentlemen are and in what countries they are operating. After all, the best customer we have for our products is the United States, but, roughly speaking, they sell us two dollars' worth of goods for every dollar's worth that we sell them. Now, we enjoy our great volume of trade there without much solicitation on our part, and it seems strange to me that we do not adopt an aggressive trade policy in that great market right at our door instead of sending trade commissioners to remote foreign countries. The appointment of trade agents in unstinted numbers to make a drive for business in the United States would -her most opportune at this particular time, for it is acknowledged by all economists that the only way to put ourselves as nearly as possible on a par of exchange with that great country is by increasing the volume of our exports there. The history of the United States after the Civil War shows most conclusively that they tackled their biggest problems in the building of canals and railroads on top of the greatest debt that the country had ever shouldered. Their slogan was: Full steam ahead! It seems to me that that would be a splendid motto for us to adopt now in developing our present trade channels and opening up new ones. I cannot conceive why in the trade bulletin which goes to all members all sorts of statistics are to be found about the opportunities for trade in Asia, Europe and Africa, illustrated with beautiful pictures of temples situated on the banks of the sacred rivers of the East, and of gondolas on the Venetian canals, while the possibilities of trade with over one hundred millions of people right at our door are apparently ignored. My hon. friend says that the United States has eighty-four consular agents and subsidiary officers here- although I think he would be nearer the mark if he stated the number at fifty-two- all active, energetic men pushing the sale of United States goods in Canada, while we are left to the tender mercies of the British

consular agents in the United States. What do the latter care for the trade of Canada? They are in the United States for the purpose of increasing the trade of England, Ireland and Scotland. Undoubtedly the English people are the greatest traders in the world. They are alive to the necessity of keeping their mercantile marine busy, and they do it through the medium of foreign trade.- Here we are, close to that. vast market with only an imaginary boundary line between us, and it is scarcely credible that the Administration will send its trade agents to foreign climes, thousands of miles away, and neglect the American market right at our door. The minister says that his trade agents abroad are very satisfactory, but I have a recollection of being in the office of one of those gentlemen -I will give his name to the minister privately, as it is something I do not like to speak of publicly. This was some years ago before the present minister was in charge of the Department of Trade and Commerce. I saw the sign, and I went in and interviewed the commissioner, purely out of my desire as a Canadian to know what was going on in relation to Canadian trade. He was a kindly gentleman and a pleasant conversationalist, but before leaving he asked me if I could get for him at Ottawa a map of Canada to put upon his office wall. I said, "Surely you have a map?" He replied, "No, and I need one very much." He also wished me to send him a little atlas which the Canadian Government published and which would be more convenient to him than a map when giving information to callers about Canada and her resources. On my return home I sent him the map and atlas. I am sure that had that been brought to the attention of the right hon. minister who is now head of the department it in itself would have caused a shaking up of the dry bones of the trade commissioners who represent Canada, and would have led to the fitting out of their offices in such a manner as would enable them to talk intelligently about the country they represent and to give to prospective traders all the information likely to promote Canadian trade.
not only information about goods but where the people are and who can supply them- how far it is from Montreal, how far from Toronto and so on. The minister may suggest that surely the trade agent knew that. Well, he had not a map by which to explain it to anybody, and he needed it. It does seem to me that the department should take for its motto: "Full steam ahead." These 
trade commissioners should be properly equipped and informed as to what is necessary in the best interests of our country. Moreover, there should be established at points such as -those referred to by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) independent Canadian trade agents for the express purpose of working in Canada's interests. I have heard no objections to the adoption of that course. The remarks of the hon. member for Parkdale with regard to the expense are much to the point. The fees received by the United States consular agents are, I gather from his remarks, sufficient to pay all the expenses of the American offices here. Surely it would be advisable to try it out, establishing only a few offices at first at the most advantageous points on the other side. The fact that we are doing $500,000,000 worth of trade or thereabouts each year with the United States is in itself an assurance that the cost of establishing and maintaining the offices would be made up by fees, as is the case with the United States offices in Canada. In other words, the offices of these Canadian trade agents would be practically self-sustaining. I leave that suggestion with the minister-full steam ahead on the specific line of the development of Canadian trade, making the Canadian seller of goods, the Canadian wholesaler, the Canadian manufacturer, feel that he has the loyal and active co-operation and assistance of the Government. Even if he is slow himself, he would give the Government credit for having pointed the way to the development and expansion of trade. Moreover, the adoption of this course and the resulting increase of trade would soon have the effect of adjusting the balance of trade as between Canada and the United States.

Mr. Chairman, "full steam ahead " is an excellent motto if you accompany it with another: " Be sure you are right, then go ahead." I need hardly say I sympathize most heartily with every effort to improve our trade relations with the United States; therefore the object that the member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) has in view is one with which I am in accord. But I am inclined to think that the argument in favour of trade agents in the United States is not as strong as some people think it is. There is very much force in the view advanced by the minister that one of the reasons why we do not need trade agents in the United States is because we are so near to that country. My hon. friend from Perth (Mr. Morphy) thinks that the fact that we are so near to them is a rea-

son why we should have trade agents there. But you need trade agents in distant ports because distant ports have no convenient means of communicating with us.

Not only does the
United States have consular agents in Canada, but our country is overrun with their commercial travellers.

Is there any reason why we should not have commercial travellers in the United States? Do our merchants and manufacturers need Government assistance in the matter of sending their travellers to the United States? I do think, however, that the argument in favour of the maintaining of trade agents in distant countries which are not conveniently in communication with Canada is a strong one.

The reason why the
commercial travellers come here from the United States is because the trade agents of the United States tell them what they can sell here-encourage them and bring them here.

Oh no, it is because they learn from the morning newspaper all about Canada. Of course, in exceptional cases trade agents might advantageously be maintained in certain parts of the United States. The member for Parkdale suggested New Orleans, which is rather distant from Canada. There might be exceptional circumstances under which our having a trade agent at a particular point would be useful, and so far from discouraging it I would cordially support the minister in adopting any suggestion of that kind. But the idea that we should have these trade agents all over the United States is open to the gravest objection. A man who wants to do business between New York and Montreal does not need any trade agents; he can get nearly all the information he wants for a postage stamp, or he can leave by the evening train and arrive in Montreal on the morning of the next day, and vice versa. I am persuaded that the business relations between Canada and the United States will be almost as good without trade agents as with them, unless under such exceptional conditions as I have mentioned. It is my recollection that years ago we had a trade agent in Chicago. We found that he was not needed; that he was not accomplishing anything of a practical nature, and I believe that he was sent to some other part of the country. If you appoint seventy or eighty agents of Canada in the United States and
they collect fees on American goods coming in, as is suggested, that will be an additional tax upon the Canadian people who bring the goods in. Whether we want them to bring those goods in is another question. It is their liberty to do so; the tariff permits it. But if you have a large army of Canadian agents in the United States and bring about the imposition of that additional tax, it may suit some interests in the country but it will not suit the consumer. It may be said that the object of maintaining these trade agents is to check the exports and adjust the balance of trade. Well, I do not think that is the best way to do it. We do not want to impose unnecessary taxation upon any part of our people. I repeat that in special cases, such as at New Orleans or other distant ports-even, perhaps, at New York or Boston-we might well have trade agents, but the idea of having a large army of them in the United States ought not to be too readily accepted. I am rather in sympathy with the view expressed by the minister that our proximity to the United States is one of the reasons why we do not need an army of agents in that country.

The hon. gentleman is most delightful in exaggerating to suit his own purpose. I have not yet heard any one speak about a "large army" of trade agents. I purposely suggested the advisability of starting with a few agents with a view to determining the advantages of the plan. I admit that the hon. gentleman has had vast experience and it is with diffidence that I dispute his suggestion in regard to this matter. But I have come across Americans who do not know this country as we know the United States- people who believe that this is a country of ice and snow, a country of Indians and bears. I am not sure that it would not be a good thing for Canada to send a moving picture show to the United States with a view to depicting the activities in our large cities, the beauty and extent of our lakes and rivers, the value of our steamship services, and so on-in short, to educate those people down there who are apparently backward so far as a knowledge of Canada is concerned.
Our railways.

Our railways would also be an object lesson. Why, some people who plan to visit Canada in the summer think that they are coming to the frigid zone and that they should bring their winter

clothes; the fact is that they do not know us. These trade agents would make them know us, wo.uld make them know our trade capacity, would do a great many things. The hon. gentleman speaks about a large army; I want to remind him that this is not war time. That is not language that is justifiable in answer to what I have stated as a matter of principle. Nobody is talking about a "large army," an expression that was repeated three or four times-by the hon. gentleman. My idea is to attempt to establish the principle of expansion of trade in that way. I asked the minister definitely and specifically if he did not wish to take a number of men and put them in that position to try to work out that scheme. The United States to-day is filled with the brightest brains of Canada in the services of banking, railways and other activities. Is it to be said that Canada cannot send men to expand our trade, when the United States is draining our country of some of the best brains we have for some of its greatest activities? I am surprised that the hon. gentleman has so little faith in the ability of our young men. I can safely point to the cities of Halifax, Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver, and I can pick out fifty men as bright as any commercial agent that ever lived, who could go out and do equally good work for Canada as these United States agents are doing here. It is not right to belittle the idea that we have potentialities in our manufactures in Canada.

Would it not be better for us to establish trade commissioners at home ' to take that billion dollars worth of trade the Americans get here at the expense of our manufacturers? That would be starting the business at home.

That is a general principle with which I think both sides of the House would agree, but they may fail to agree upon the proper method of carrying it out. They have failed to come together on a straight national policy. I am prone to think, and I want to say right now, that one of the weaknesses in our Canadian national life is the fact that while in this chamber there are men, who believe in a certain policy for the welfare, expansion, growth and swelling of the activities of Canada, for those things that will go to bring us above the debt that burdens us, the one thing in the way is partisanship 
on the part of men who will surrender their conviction for the sake of the fetish of a party name. Men on the other side, ardent protectionists, willing to build up the country in that way, will vote for a reduction in the tariff in order to get into office.

The zeal of my hon.
friend (Mr. Morphy) in favour of better relations with the United States is exceedingly interesting. I will not say it is amusing, because that would not be courteous to my hon. friend. I will not say it is surprising, although I might say that in view of certain events which occurred not very long ago. My hon. friend had something to say about men belittling the young men of the country. I do not know who did so, I certainly have not said anything of the sort. If there are these hundreds and thousands of able young men throughout the country, by all means let them go to the United States as commercial travellers or anything else, if they are wanted. I believe they can go without any Government assistance. The only portion of my hon. friend's remarks with which I can agree is that of advertising Canada by films and so forth. He must have been asleep or absent this afternoon and evening; otherwise he would have known that my right hon. friend (Sir George Foster) explained at great length this afternoon that the Government are doing that now. It is a good service, I commend my right hon. friend for doing it. I am willing to accept the assurance of the minister that he is doing it now. My hon. friend seems to assume that the minister is not doing it and that some movement of that kind is necessary.
I was absent this afternoon when that information was given to the committee. I was not aware of it.
I thought not.

I do not know that there was any crime in my not being in the House at the moment. As to the gratuitous suggestion of my being asleep in the House, that is a pleasure which, since I have been a member of the House of Commons, I have never once enjoyed.

You do not know what
you have missed.

I hope hon. gentlemen
opposite have as clean a sheet upon that subject as I. The point that I make is merely fringed by what the hon. gentleman

said a little time ago about commercial travellers. I would organize them or have the State take it upon itself to organize them as commercial agents and send them out. That is the difference between the hon. gentleman and myself. He is willing to admit the value of the trade and ardently desires the trade. I ardently desire to get it. The only difference is that he does not agree with the principle of the Government assisting to develop Canadian trade. What is the Department of Trade and Commerce for, unless it is for that very thing, 

the development of the trade of Canada for the benefit of the people of Canada? If that be so, we have at our doors a market of 100,000,000 people who are crowding upon us and selling and dumping their goods upon us, through the activities of their trade agents and consular officers, but we are pusillanimous enough to say:
. "We will not do the same thing; we will go to them."

I am sorry to dissent from my hon. friend. He intimates that I am complaining of the Government. He is complaining of the Government; I am commending the Minister of Trade and Commerce for what he is doing. The hon. gentleman is doing his best to make it appear that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is neglecting his work. I am standing by the Government in this matter; my hon. friend is attacking them.
I am attacking the Government in this way: I believe it is the duty of every member of this House who has opinions, to express them freely.
Except when there is a vote on.	.
I do not know that that is an exception that it is' not wise to follow when you have on one side of the House-
The patriots.

The hon. gentleman
may have a right to talk about patriotism. He himself has it, but it is coming pretty close to some hon. members opposite who dare not say very much about it.
As much as the other side.

As to the vote, I have shown independence in this House in voting occasionally against the Government. I would like to know if the hon. gentleman ever did so in his life. Nobody ever heard of his doing so. He has been a party slave.

I have always voted
against the Government.

That is pretty cheap and very well put in. I meant against the hon. gentleman's leader and party and policy. He knew very well what I meant. People who live in glass houses should not throw stones. I am not attacking the Government because the Government has not inaugurated this policy. There is no attack about the matter; I want them to carry out this policy; that is all.

There has been more or less discussion about charges made by consular agents of the United States. Wrhat are their charges for? When I have gone to export goods to the United States, I have never heard of being charged by them.

Before I answer that question, I want to address a word to my hon. friend (Mr. Morphy), who has spoken so eloquently to-night. I am afraid he has been asleep a bit. I am inclined to agree with my hon. friend opposite (Mr. Fielding) that he does occasionally take a nap.	[DOT]
No.
If not in the House, certainly somewhere else.
Not while the House is in session.

My hon.'friend charged me and the Government because we were so dilatory that we did not give the names of our trade commissioners, and he thought I might at least get up and read them. Then, afterwards, he showed an intimate acquaintance with the bulletins. He had looked at the Ganges as it was portrayed in the bulletin, had seen a sacred temple here and Bangkok there, but he never knew, and does not know now, who our trade commissioners are, though every edition of the bulletin has the names of every one of our trade commissioners, and where they are stationed. If my hon. friend would just read that page of the bulletin he would have that information.
I have seen the names, but I want them put on record so that the country will know them.
The country sees them as well as my hon. friend. They are everywhere throughout the country.
Oh, no, they are not.

There is not a business house in this country that has not the bulletin on its table, and that does

not know where every one of our trade agents is stationed.
That is right.

There is not a trade commissioner in the service now who does not visit Canada once in every two years and make a tour of the whole Dominion from one end to the other; he talks with the merchants and manufacturers, interchanges information, gets the information that he needs, and goes back again to his field with the best possible equipment that can be given to him. My hon. friend was unfair to the service in resuscitating ancient history to the extent of giving a description of a trade commissioner of this Government who had not a map of Canada in his office and had to ask my hon. friend for a copy. That must have been in the dim and dusty ages of long ago. I do not think my hon. friend could find such a trade commissioner now. It rather grates on the commissioners, who are putting their best efforts into their work of securing trade for Canada along the most instructed and best possible lines, to be held up in the House of Commons as of the same type as that antediluvian of whom my hon. friend spoke, and who had to ask him for a map and a book that he wanted. All our agents are thoroughly furnished, all who are in the field now are intelligent men, and I believe that the exceptions are very few where these men are not absolutely devoted to their work and doing it with a spirit and elan which is entirely satisfactory. I have more to do with them than has my hon. friend, and when he gets a little leisure and goes out into foreign countries, I want him to go into the offices of our trade commissioners and talk with the men who are performing this service, and I know when he comes back he will have a higher opinion of them.
Now, let us come back for a moment to the stationing of the men in the United States. We have to do it on a wholesale plan if it is to be made self-supporting. You cannot place an agent in New York, or New Orleans, pay him by charges which he is authorized to make upon invoice of goods shipped from his locality, and not treat other parts of the United States where we trade in the very same way. It would not be fair to our own merchants; it would not be fair in any sense. We would in that case have to foot the whole

expense, and not	charge it upon
the United States.	I do not think
there is any getting away from that, and that is one thing I want hon. members to think over as one of the difficulties in the way. It must be a wholesale business or none. We have to put at least one or two hundred men in the United States to cover the vast area where our people do business. The business is so widely distributed that you cannot mark off a little zone in one part of the United States, say to every man who trade from Canada in that zone that he must pay $2.50 on every invoice, or three per cent on the value of the goods, or whatever it is, and not subject his competitor who buys from other parts of the United States to the very same charge, because it is said in the United States, and it will be said with us, that it is really the purchaser in the United States who has to pay this invoice charge. But the matter does not go only that far. We must also take foreign countries into account. Some foreign countries do the same as the United States. They charge upon the invoice, either a percentage of its value, or a certificate of charge. A number of countries do that. These are some of the things we have to take into account.
In reply to the question of my hon, friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), the United States consuls certificate the invoice and charge $2.50, whether the invoice is for $200 or $20,000. Other countries, the South American States particularly, follow a different plan. There are two or three of them that make a flat charge, but the others make a percentage charge of from 1 to 3 per cent upon the value of the goods. France has a flat charge, I think, and some other countries a percentage charge. It is a large subject, and I have mentioned a few of the things that we must consider before we jump into it. That is what I and the Government are trying to do before making up our minds as to the policy to be adopted. I am quite in accord with my hon. friend as to the necessity of being alive and active.
My hon. friend also alluded to publicity by means of films, evidently without the knowledge that we had been engaged in that work for a couple of years, and were pushing it. As I said this afternoon, there are probably three or four millions of people who in the United States see these films depicting our sources, our productive processes, the beauties of our scenery, and everything in connection therewith. They

are learning of Canada through the eye, and what is learnt in this way impresses itself on the mind. Every picture has a title which fixes on the mind one important fact with reference to what is being shown. It is a fine way of cultivating the interest and of expanding the knowledge of people.

I was very much interested in the remarks made by my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy). As I listened, approving to a certain extent the remarks which he delivered this evening, I thought of ten years ago and asked myself, how it is that the hon. gentleman has reversed so completely his policy? I suppose, Mr. Chairman, that if in the year 1911 you and I, belonging to the same party and to the same league, had been suddenly transported to the beautiful county of Perth we would probably have heard very different sentiments from those the hon. gentleman has expressed here to-night. My hon. friend is most anxious now to develop trade with the United States. We should have, he says, young Canadian emissaries in every centre of American activity from east to west and north to south, and our motto should be the old Yankee motto after the Civil War, "Full steam ahead." We should attract American capital , to Canada, and boost Canada in the U. S. What a change of heart, Mr. Chairman! Why, I am sure that the hon. members opposite in 1911, with the right hon. gentleman leading the chorus-
I do not sing.

Probably not the swan
song; but the right hon. minister had a ebautiful clarion voice in 1911, and he sang the well known refrain: "No truck nor trade with the Yankees" and "Under which flag?" Canada first, Canada last, and Canada for ever!" By the way, I would suggest to my hon. friend from Perth that the real motto of our trade agents in the U.S. should be, not "full speed ahead,'" but the old Macdonald motto, the old Blake motto:	"Canada
first." That would be my motto in the United States of America. Mr. Chairman, trade will find its level just as water will, and it is not through a high tariff wall that you will attract trade to your country. There was, in 1911, a splendid and unique opportunity for Canada to develop a sound, healthy and prosperous trade with the United States. We had sought for that opportunity since the abrogation of the
first reciprocity treaty in 1866. Sir John A. Macdonald in 1872, Mr. George Brown in 1874, Sir John Macdonald again in 1879, Sir Charles Tupper, and my right hon. friend, in 1891, indeed, all the leaders of public opinion on both sides of politics, for practically half a century, clamoured and clamoured in vain for the return of the golden era between 1854 and 1866. And in 1898, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the last of our great statesmen who have disappeared from public life, after vain efforts to renew that reciprocity treaty, said at last: We shall make no more pilgrimages to Washington.
In the year 1910 the hon. gentleman sitting beside me (Mr. Fielding), who presided over the Treasury Department, having made a great name for himself as Minister of Finance, was invited for the first time in the history of our relations with the United States, to go, not to Washington, but to meet half way, at Albany, I believe, the representatives of the American Government with a view to securing to the United States the benefit of a reciprocity pact with Canada. He came back with the very same offer-there were perhaps a few items, more or less, changed, but it was practically the same-which had been on our statute book since 1879, because the National Policy, of which the right hon. gentleman is so proud, was based on a permanent standing offer of reciprocity in natural products with the United States. If my hon. friend will refer to the statute of 1879, he will see, in black and white, that the National Policy was launched with a view to obtaining a reciprocity pact with the United States. In that statute there is a permanent standing offer of reciprocity with them in natural products. My hon. friend, I say, went to the United States, where he met the chief of the executive and succeeded in obtaining from their Government a pact which no one can deny was the best commercial agreement ever reached by us with the United States. When it was presented to Parliament it was received with applause on both sides of the House. It made for better relations with the Republic to the south of us, not only in trade matters, but socially as well. We cannot forget that they are our neighbours and it is well for us to have cordial relations with them.
But the right hon. gentleman and my hon. friend from Perth (Mr. Morphy) were among the chief offenders in '1911. From	one end	of the country
to the other they abused the United



States and the American people, and, not satisfied with that, they accused the great statesman who had negotiated the agreement, as well as his fellow-workers in the Canadian Government of being traitors. We know what the result was, because you and I, Mr. Chairman, were of the minority elected on that policy in 1911. Now, I repeat, if you wish to develop trade with the United States, the larger part of that business being agricultural,- because Canada is a great farming country [DOT]-what is most essential is a market for our farm products. The manufacturers can take care of themselves. We have a great many manufacturing establishments in the province of Ontario and in Quebec, and I know that to a certain extent, from statistics available, they can compete in many lines even with the Americans. The trade which we must promote the most is that of our agricultural products with the United States. I am afraid that it must be said of my right hon. friend, as it was said of the statesmen of Europe in the last century who were responsible for the criminal partition of Poland, that since 1911 he has been in a state of mortal sin, because he helped by word of mouth, aye by incendiary speeches, to defeat the reciprocity pact that would have provided so much business for Canada.
If that agreement were in effect to-day, we should not have the adverse balance of trade which has been deplored in a way that ill became a Canadian minister who spoke in New York the other day. By the way, I do not think it is the proper way of improving our relations with the Americans, either commercially, politically, or socially, for any of our ministers to bewail at meetings there the fact that we are buying too much from the United States. I did not like the attitude of the right hon. gentleman at that New York banquet a few weeks ago; he is usually better inspired. Nor do I like the speeches of his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), who keeps on repeating to our good people not to buy from the Americans. That is not a position of which a Canadian minister can be proud. No:	The blunder was made in
1911, when a campaign of prejudice was preached in the back concessions to defeat the commercial agreement between Canada and our great neighbour to the south. A flag-flapping campaign was organized and vigorously executed to defeat that arrangement. I can remember that some farmers from the province of Ontario,

when they heard that a reciprocity pact had been negotiated, sent telegram after telegram of congratulations to my hon. friend, some of them affirming that the value of their farms would be doubled and trebled by the effect of that agreement. Sir, do you not see to-day that the wave of discontent and unrest which exists in the great farming communities of Canada, in Ontario and in the West, is due largely to the treacherous policy in 1911, of the party that faces me to-night? Why did you prevent the Canadian farmer from selling his products? The pact did not affect the manufacturers. You have created grievances which to-day have come back with a vengeance. This is plain talk, but the right hon. gentleman knows that I am speaking the unvarnished truth.
Now, as to the campaign against the United States. If you wish to promote trade with the United States, if you are so anxious to get an export market for Canadian products in that counti'y, why do not hon. gentlemen opposite stop the campaign of vilification against the Americans-carried on here in the city of Ottawa, there in the city of Toronto? I have here a review which is published under the auspices of the Government party nailed The Onlooker. What do I read in that review? My hon. friend from Perth wishes to send Canadian trade agents into the United States. I wonder if the following from The Onlooker of March, 1921, is conducive to better trade relations with the Americans:
At the back of the brain of the average American there lies the conviction that sooner or later but one flag will fly over the whole surface of the North American continent from the North Pole to the Isthmus of Panama. He calls it, and has called it for years, "Inevitable Destiny". We do not blame him. The genuine native-born American has many lovable qualities. . . . The danger may not be immediate, but in dim outline it already looms vast on the national horizon and fills some of us with apprehension.
Reference is made to the designs, "the sinister designs" of the average American against Canada. Further on the article says:
It is not the cultivated American, half of whose heart, and almost the whole of whose culture, is in Britain, we dread. It is not spiritual and intellectual America we fear. It is commercial America we doubt. For commerce is impersonal, without sentiment, and takes no cognizance of those higher things that illuminate and enrich the national life. So far, indeed, as the soul is concerned, gold is the deadliest of narcotics.	* *
The true danger lies in scarcely recognized impersonal tendencies with which kindly ex-

pressions of goodwill have little or nothing to do.
My hon. friend can see to what danger he is exposing himself and his good people when he wants to get American gold. It is the "deadliest of narcotics" says this Tory publication. Mr. Chairman, let us be frank about this matter. The Americans, when the test came were at one with the British Empire, were at one with the Allies in upholding the cause of civilization and liberty. They have with us practically a common history, common laws, a common language and common ideals. I am speaking of the majority in both countries. What is the object of that pinpricking policy which is aided and subsidized by the funds of a certain party? Do you think you will promote Canadian trade with the Americans by publishing such vicious appeals as these? As to the merits of trade representation in the United States I am inclined to believe that it would not be a bad thing if there were some trade agents in the principal centres of the United States. I do not say that we should have trade agents in every city or town; but there are large centres like Chicago, St. Paul, Minneapolis, New Orleans, New York and Boston where there should be Canadian trade agents. We were told by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) not long ago, that Canada was a nation, and that so soon as it pleased this country she might appoint consular agents, and even an ambassador at Washington. Why do we not appoint consular agents if we have that potential power? If there is a country in the world where we are interested in having consular agents it is the United States of America. I do not know how it is with my friends of English parentage, but I know as regards those of my nationality, there are in the United States not as many French Canadians as there are in the province of Quebec, but there are certainly over a million and a half of them in that country. The largest French centres, outside of Montreal and Quebec, are in the New England cities- cities like Lowell, Manchester, Boston, Bay City and others. All these cities are large French Canadian centres. There is a coming and going of French Canadians all the time between these cities and our province, and it is strange to think that the invoices and the passports necessitated by that ebb and flow of people have to go before the British consul when we could have a consular agent of our own to look 941
after these matters. As a matter of fact I know, because I have often accepted invitations from Canadian clubs in the United States, that Philadelphia, for instance, is simply an outpost for Toronto, Hamilton and London, as Boston is an outpost for Halifax and St. John. In New York, in Boston, there are at least twenty-five to thirty thousand Canadians. So we are closely connected with the Republic, and it is ngt by such writings as the one I have just read to the committee that we will improve our relations, commercial and otherwise, with the Americans. Remember, Mr. Chairman, that the first trade treaty of 1854 with the United States was negotiated at a time when it meant the salvation of Canada from a national point of view. Remember that the first reciprocity treaty was negotiated with the United States when there was in this country a strongly expressed sentiment in favour of annexation on account of the removal of the British preference following on the establishment [DOT] of free trade in England. The annexation manifesto was not signed by rebels like myself or like my friends from Gloucester, Vaudreuil and Joliette, it was signed by Sir John Abbott. Sir John Rose, Sir A. T. Galt, Judge Johnson of Montreal-indeed by the best English stock in Canada, by our great merchants and captains of industry. That manifesto was remarkably well drafted. It was transmitted by Lord Elgin to the British authorities, and he warned them that if immediate action was not taken there was a grave danger that Canada would pass under the political domination of the United States. He was at once authorized by the British Government to himself go to Washington and negotiate a treaty. He succeeded in his mission, and that treaty lasted until 1866. We know why it was abrogated:	In those days-as to-day unfortunately-there was a class of Canadians always ready to belittle the Americans and to speak of them in uncomplimentary terms. Some of the confederate victories were applauded even in the Canadian Parliament. As a result, when, after the 'civil war, the time came to renew the treaty the _ Americans	refused. Since 1866
men in both our great parties, men occupying the position of my right hon. friend (Sir George Foster) and the position of my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) have tried in vain to secure the renewal of that treaty. Our statesmen went periodically to Washington with that end in view-Sir John A. MacDonald at the time of the Fisheries Treaty,

the Hon. George Brown, Sir Charles Tupper, my right hon. friend, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Sir Richard Cartwright -because by them all, it was considered that the renewal of that trade agreement would be in the best interests of Canada. Ultimately my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's succeeded-but not at his asking. He was solicited by the Americans themselves, by Mr. Taft and Mr. Knox, to enter into a trade compact in natural products. But, unfortunately for Canada, there was a party in this House and in the country which was more anxious to defeat the Liberal government than to give the farmers the great market which Canda had been seeking for upwards of fifty years. Now my right hon. friend is anxious to secure business from the United States. Let him make a confession, and let him have contrition for the mortal sin he committed in 1911. Then we will give him another lease of office, if need be, in order that he may redeem his soul by improving the trade relations between Canada and the great republic to the south of us. I agree that it is not natural that Canada should have this enormous balance of trade against her; the Americans should buy much more than they do from their best customer. The best means towards attaining this worthy object, is to get the American market for our farmers and i know of no better man than the right hon. gentleman to do. the trick, if he will undertake it.

Mr. Chairman, we listened this afternoon to attempts to blacken the record of the little angularly opposite group here in connection with the items that came before this committee. We took part in that discussion, and I do not think it is necessary to follow up any further this political cross-firing. The subject with which we are now dealing is worthy of the most careful consideration. I quite agree with my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) that the best way to accomplish what we require here, if I interpret his view correctly, is by some reciprocal arrangement with the United States. I am satisfied that we will never secure proper trade relations except in that way. However, we have to take conditions as we find them, and we must recognize that while the present Government retain power it is hopeless to expect any move in that direction. As we are not in a position to set to work in the best way, we must adopt the second best, and I am still of the opinion that lies in endeavouring to secure a reception for exports to the United States

through trade commissioners. The right hon. gentleman has held up the horrible picture of the necessity of one or two or possibly three hundred trade commissioners to carry out this plan, while the hon. member for Maisonneuve seems to think we might start with a small number. I would be sorry to advance my opinion against gentlemen of such great experience, but as they hold entirely different views I may venture to express the opinion that there is no reason why we cannot start work with a small number of trade commissioners. The hon. member for Maisonneuve has spoken of the necessity of cultivating a market in the United States for our farm products, and I agree with him that that is the only kind of trade which will help us to get rid of the present adverse balance of trade. It is natural that we should supply farm products to our neighbours to the south, and perhaps it is quite as natural that they should supply us with some other things which they can manufacture more cheaply. To my mind any effort to develop along unnatural lines is not likely to succeed. The best and only way of developing trade is along natural lines, that is, to purchase those things which can be more cheaply manufactured in other countries, and to export to those countries things which we can produce more cheaply. We have shown our ability to produce farm products as well as any country in the world, and better than our neighbours to the south. Our manufacturers tell us that it is utterly impossible for them to manufacture as cheaply as their competitors in the United States. I do not agree with that. Anyway, it is quite plain that in cultivating profitable trade with our American neighbours we must endeavour to sell to them as much as possible of our farm produce. I daresay that the efforts of our trade commissioners have largely been directed towards the procuring of markets for our manufactured articles, and that is because of the mad notion we have that that is the only way in which the country can be developed. I say it is a mad notion, and the sooner we get rid of it the better. The . sooner we come to understand that we should export the things which we can most profitably produce, the better for us and for the world at large.
It is quite plain that we can improve our trade relations with certain countries by means of trade agents, because we are employing them now in different parts of the world. The Americans, who are a

shrewd commercial people, believe that they can improve their trade relations in contiguous countries by the appointment of trade agents. They are not spending this money for the pure love of spending it; they believe that they will get some benefit from the expenditure. Possibly one of the reasons for our adverse balance of trade with the United States is found in the fact that the United States is appointing trade agents to look after its export trade to Canada while Canada is making no effort to increase her exports to the United States. I understood the minister to say before six o'clock that the Government were considering this matter. If so, this is the proper time for us to air our views. I am sure that the right hon. gentleman will not be averse to receiving suggestions even from back benchers in this unfortunate group which has been so much abused this afternoon.
Item agreed to.

Before we proceed to another item I want to refer to item 361, which I understand was passed at a late hour last night. I suppose un'der that item would be included the printing of blue books. In one very useful book issued by the Finance Department, the Public Accounts, there had been published from Confederation up to last year tables of expenditure from the Consolidated Revenue Fund in the various departments, and by one glance at these pages the growth of our expenditure in all the various departments could be readily ascertained. In the issue of the book for 1920 these tables were eliminated, on the ground, as is stated in the first part of the report, of economy. I understand that my right hon. friend is a member of the committee that controls the printing of blue books, and that is the reason why I mention the matter now. I would like him to consider the restoration of these tables. They have been very useful to me and I know that they have been regarded as valuable by many members of the House as well as by men who are not in the House. Year after year I have been asked to send this book to people who value the information that had been given in these tables. Only a few leaves have been cut out by eliminating them, and I certainly think it is false economy. I trust that the minister will take the trouble to look into it, and if he agrees with, me, to see that when the book comes out next year these tables are restored.

I certainly will look into it.
Weights and Measures, salaries of inspectors, and staff, $192,460; rent, fuel, travelling expenses, postage, stationery, etc., $125,000; International Bureau of Weights and Measures, $400.
What is the reason for the increase?

It is due
mainly to the reclassification. There is an increase also in contingent expenses for travelling, owing to the fact that we now carry out the inspection of weights and measures throughout the country every year, whereas we formerly did it once in two years. Last year or the year before we increased the fees. When this branch came over to my department I found a surplus of officials, and as some of the older officers are retired they are not being replaced. As a result of these considerations the Weights and Measures Branch for part of the year just passed has for the first time shown a surplus over expenditure. WTe think, therefore, that we are on the way to making this branch pay for itself.

Item agreed to.
Mail subsidies and steamship subventions- Atlantic Ocean-Canada and Newfoundland, steam service or services between, $35,000.
Has the Government commission in charge of the Newfoundland railways, which are really a part of this service, brought about any betterment of the road or any general improvement of the system?

I am afraid I cannot say that matters with reference to the railway are being improved. My hon. friend, perhaps, knows something of the situation as regards that road. Newfoundland has had the hardest winter it has had for many years. The road has been practically out of commission for weeks at a time. The company have not entered into any contract yet for steamship service, although they are performing a service between Port aux Basques and North Sydney. They have been pressing us for a larger subsidy. The service is going on, and some of our own vessels have, I think, been put on for part of the time, but the condition of the railroad makes the service very unsatisfactory. I understand, by report, that a commission has been appointed to take into consideration the rearrangement or betterment of the road, but the situation is not very satisfactory at the present time.

I notice, in his annual report, in connection with the Canadian Merchant Marine, the minister states:

Since tlie commencement of the overseas Government service up to the 31st March, last, 71 voyages have been performed.
And in that number I notice that seven voyages have been performed between Canada and Newfoundland. How are these subsidies entered into? Are they entered into for a term of years? It seems rather inconsistent for us to be building merchant ships and sending them to Newfoundland and also subsidizing vessels of other lines which are apparently competitors. As the Canadian Merchant Marine increases and grows strong, will these subsidies cease and will we do our own work between Canada and Newfoundland?

I have not the management of the Canadian Merchant Marine, and none of my appropriations go to the merchant marine, as my hon. friend knows. That is carrying on its services, and it has put on certain services between Halifax and St. John's, Newfoundland. It is putting on some services between Quebec and Newfoundland during the summer season, but neither of those touches this route, which is the link between the end of our Canadian National railways and the terminus of the Newfoundland railway at Port aux Basques.
Why could we not use our own boats to make this connecting link?
We have not used them.
Why should we not?
I do not know that they would be exactly fitted for that service. Anyway we have reduced the vote by $30,000. *
What became of the old Bruce?
She came to grief some way or another, I do not know where.
Are these contracts for subsidies made for a term of years or just for one year?
This one is made ' from year to year.
Would it not be a good thing for the minister to look into the question whether it would not be wise to cut off this subsidy and use our own boats? They would not be all too busy.

I have looked into that, and in some cases we have taken off the subsidy where our boats are doing

the work to-day. You cannot make all these substitutions at once. I am not sure whether our own boats can be used on this route at all. That, however, is a matter to be considered.

I am afraid that the cutting down of this subsidy has rather paralyzed this service. For quite a number of years, as the minister knows, the Reid Newfoundland company was getting a subsidy of $70,000, and with that subsidy, the water end of the service was carried on very satisfactorily; they carried many passengers and large quantities of freight between the terminus of the National railways at North Sydney and Newfoundland. But ever since this cut was made, things have been paralyzed. There are no proper boats where there used to be a daily service and two boats on continuously. I think my right hon. friend will find that there is only one boat now, the Kyle, that can really be called a boat that is fitted for the service. The Reid Newfoundland company contend that they cannot enter into a contract to carry the mails, but the mails between Canada and Newfoundland are very large. As far as I know, they go from North Sydney to Port aux Basques, or when they cannot go to Port aux Basques, they go to St. John's. It is rather a serious thing so to cut this subsidy as to strike a blow at an old service like this. This route was established some twenty-five years ago when the first Bruce was built. The first Bruce was lost, and the second Bruce, which was an equally good boat, was commandeered by the British Government and sent to Russia as an icebreaker during the war. She has never come back, and I suppose she became a Russian boat long ago.
