The company would like to get a satisfactory condition again as they had before the war to carry on the service, and I am afraid that this cutting the subsidy by one-half is not going to enable us to have that service. My home town is the terminus of the road and the starting point for trade with Newfoundland. When I talk about that service, people might think I am talking about my home town, but the service is of very little advantage to us. The boat comes and goes; travellers land at North Sydney and take passage to all parts of the world; large quantities of freight come and are switched down to the wharf and the stuff goes on to the boat and off to Newfoundland. The service means very little to us, but nevertheless it is a magnificent source of trade. Our Canadian trade with Newfoundland is very large, and unless we have

proper means of handling it, we cannot hope to keep it going. If a man in Newfoundland buys a few cars of flour and they stand for six weeks on the wharf at North Sydney and are not taken across to meet the necessities of his trade, he is not very likely to repeat his order in that way. We have keen competition from Americans who have water advantages that we have not. When I bring this matter to the attention of the minister and of the Government, it is not a local matter at all; it is the broad question of Canadian trade with a British country such as Newfoundland is, a country that is willing to trade with us. It came out the other day that we were competing with ourselves. We are competing with ourselves in this trade by putting on boats at Halifax and carrying stuff from that port to Newfoundland instead of letting it all go by the one route. I can readily understand that the Government boats are not fit for the trade between Port aux Basques and North Sydney, so far as passengers are concerned, but they can certainly carry freight. I have been in conversation with the minister several times about the betterment of the terminus at Norh Sydney. This is not a local niatter at all. It is a matter of just as much concern to the man who ships a carload of flour from Manitoba to Newfoundland as it is to the people of North Sydney, that there should be proper facilities at the terminus of the road for handling the business- that goes there. For the last three years, at all events, we have been promised from day to day that the wharves would be extended and that better facilities would be provided at that point. So far I have not heard this year whether that is to be done or not, and I am simply doing my duty in bringing this matter to the notice of the Department of Trade and Commerce, which seems to be particularly the one that functions along this line. If the people of Canada find that their trade with Newfoundland is falling off, they will know that the cause to some extent is that we are not in a proper position to handle expeditiously the traffic that now exists, and that has been growing very satisfactorily during the last 25 years. While the trade was very small at the beginning, it is very substantial now, and I hope that the minister, so far as he can do so, will see that everything is done to hold the trade we now have, and develop it as much as possible.

Repairs and improvements are now being made on our
end of the road, but the trouble is at the Port aux Basques end. The trouble is with the railway accommodation in Newfoundland itself. It has happened again and again that vessels loaded at the Sydney side have gone over to the other side and have had to bring back part of their cargo, in whole or in part, because it could not be accommodated there. The service which was meant to be a daily service when we paid the heavy subsidy is now at best a triweekly service. With poor equipment, a bad road, no accommodation at Port aux Basque's, and only a tri-weekly service, the trade is going in some respects through other channels. Our own vessels of the merchant marine are going from Halifax to St. John's, Newfoundland, which is the objective of most of the traffic. They are also putting on a service which will serve Prince Edward Island and go from there direct to St. John's, Newfoundland. Everything that can possibly be done to keep the connection on this route, I think, we have a right to do, and I am disposed to do it.

Perhaps on this item I might ask a question of the minister in reference to the new route that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries hinted the other day would be established between Montreal and Newfoundland, via Charlottetown. I take it that the intention is to go to St. John's, Newfoundland. I understand that the Board of Trade of North Sydney has been in communication with the Department of Trade and Commerce or the Department of Marine and Fisheries with a view to getting the boats to call at North Sydney or Sydney. The right hon. gentle- " man knows that in going from Charlottetown to St. John's, Newfoundland, the Isle of Cape Breton is pretty much in the track of the boat. The boats will require bunkering, of course, and instead of bunkering at Montreal or St. John's, where the price of coal is very heavy, I would submit that as a matter of business the boats should bunker at North Sydney, where they can get coal at the pit's mouth, as the saying is. As my good friend from South Cape Breton, who is now sitting beside the minister, knows, that is the spot for the boat to bunker. While there she could also take on passengers and freight for Newfoundland, and on the return voyage carry coal back from North Sydney to Montreal or Quebec. If this service is established,
I think it would be a great mistake to give the go-by to a place like North Sydney or

Sydney, where a trade could be developed, and where the boats could get the coal they need very much cheaper than at Montreal or St. John's. The coal they would get at Montreal would have come from North Sydney in the first place, and would have added to it the expense of hauling. So, as a pure matter of business, I would impress upon the minister the advisability of adopting the suggestion I have made.
That matter has already been represented and is being considered by the Mercantile Marine company, which is anxious to get all possible traffic which will pay, and to bunker at the cheapest places.

Item agreed to.
Canada and the West Indies or South America, or both, steam service or services between, $340,666.66.
Would the minister explain the present condition of tnat contract, who are the contractors, and what are the pprts of call?
The same contractors.
The Royal Mail Steam Packet company?

Yes, their contract was first for five years. Then the war intervened and we have been keeping it on from year to year. At the present time, as a part of the arrangement we are making with the West India Islands for a larger preference, there is a proposition for an improved service, and if possible, a weekly service. Of course my hon. friend knows that up to the present time everything has been at peak prices. We are simply continuing this for another year in order to give us an opportunity of getting an improved service, a weekly service if possible should the trade warrant it.

Most of our Government ships, I am aware, are only freight vessels, but I understand that in the case of at least one, if not two, of these vessels going to the West Indies passenger accommodation has been provided. Are these boats now running to the same ports as come under this item or different ports.

It is a service which runs from Halifax and St. John, Halifax mainly, to Jamaica. It touches at the Bahamas, Bermuda and British Honduras, and returns by the same route. We have had no subsidized service on that route, but as a result of the conference we had with

the West Indian delegates two vessels of the mercantile marine were fitted up with certain passenger accommodation, enough for about thirty passengers, and have been put upon that route. They will be regularly kept on that route. Jamaica and Honduras pay a certain amount. If the agreement is carried through, they bind themselves to pay a certain portion of any deficit that may occur as their contribution towards maintaining the service. Two trips have already been made, I think, and both, so far as I have learned, have been successful.
They are not in any sense competing with this line?
No; they have a different route entirely.
Do they not call at Bermuda ?

If this line
calls at Bermuda there might be some competition; just with reference to that point, and just now when it is brought to my attention, I am not sure that these steamers do call there.
They formerly did.
Yes, this line does, but the other line I have spoken of does not.
My hon. friend himself said that they went to Bermuda. I have no knowledge of the matter but I took it from what he said that the Government steamers are calling there.
I am not so certain about that, but I know that Jamaica is the chief port, and from there they go to British Honduras.
Do they go to Nassau too?
They touch at the Bahamas.
What practical advantage is there to Canada from the expenditure of this money?

This is the only regular service we have between Canada and the whole ring of West India islands and Demerara, the whole comprising the Windward and Leeward islands. It is absolutely essential to have this service if we are to promote trade between ourselves and those colonies. Whilst we have so far been carrying on this service entirely at our own expense, the West India islands touched by that route will, under the new

agreement, pay a certain proportion of the subsidy which is necessary to maintain the service.
What practical results accrue to Canada from this service? Do we get any business that we should not otherwise get? Do we sell goods there which, without the service, we could not sell?

If the hon. member will take the trouble to look over the trade returns he will find that there has been a very large increase in the total trade, both imports and exports, between ourselves and these islands.
Carried by these boats?
Yes, this is the only regular line that visits them, and it is the best service that we have ever had. The returns show the benefit of it.

I see
that Demerara is one of the ports which it is intended to serve this year.
Yes, two of the Mercantile Marine boats have been going there.
Are they under the control of the company that has the contract?
No, they are run by the Mercantile Marine.
Then the Mercantile Marine is competing with the company?
Yes.
That does not seem to be business.
It is business in one way, although in another way it introduces a complication, and it is one of the problems with which we are dealing.

It ought to be dealt
with in a sound and sensible commercial way. The same thing happened, I understand, in the service between Halifax and Newfoundland, and created considerable confusion and friction. Four companies were competing for the business between St. John's and Halifax, and the business was so small that it afforded no profit to any of the ships running on the route, but they did their best to keep the boats going. In the face of this, the Government suddenly entered the arena, and broke up the little trade there was, making it unprofitable for all concerned. There was not enough traffic to make it worth while for four companies to
operate [DOT] but they endeavoured to keep up the service and divided the work. The Government boats came in but did not reduce the freight by one cent. I am told they adopted the same schedule of freight paid to the commercial boats and simply made the business unprofitable for everyone; no one got any good but of it. Now, if that policy is to be pursued in the West Indies as well as in Newfoundland I think it is time the minister or someone in the Government took this matter into consideration. It seems to me to be very unbusinesslike to subsidize a line serving a place like Demerara and then to step in and make that line unprofitable for those who are struggling to keep it up. Nobody engaged in private business would think of doing such a thing. I hope my hon. friend will give this matter some attention and either keep the Minister of Marine away from these places or else discontinue the subsidy.

There is a
portion of the year in which it is very convenient to have extra vessels on the route. This is during the sugar season, when the amount of sugar to be moved is greater than the regular service can handle. There is the difficulty which my hon. friend speaks of, but the Mercantile Marine is bound to keep its vessels afloat and, so long as they operate, freights must be got wherever possible. So that there is in this line a competition for a certain part of the year, but these vessels prove a valuable addition during the sugar season because then there is more freight than could otherwise be moved.

This competition will make it unprofitable for the private company and next year the minister will find them asking for an increased subsidy. That is what I wish to avoid. There should be no competition of this kind. The Government have full control of the routes. My right hon. friend fixes the rates obtaining on the subsidized routes; they are submitted to him and he approves of them. So that it is not a question of rates, and if the Government step in with their boats and operate over the same lines as these subsidized vessels, the business will be unprofitable to the latter, and inevitably they
will come back for increased subsidy. I do not know whether the minister sees my point.
I see the point.
Then I hope it will be given some consideration.

The point made by my hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair), is perfectly clear. We have an item of $340,366.60 for a line to the West Indies and South America. Now, we are told that we have our own boats serving a part of that route, so that we are in competition with the vessels running there. Yet the Government is so exceedingly generous that it gives to a company with whom it is competing for trade the sum of $340,000 odd. They give them that magnificent handicap and then boldly and proudly step up and say: We will get plenty of profit notwithstanding this handicap we are giving them. Does it strike my hon. friend as good business that we should be spending $75,000,000 of the people's money in the building of boats and in looking for trade and then when we find an old service established on this route which we intend to work, instead of trying to displace those competitors, give them a subsidy? The Canadian people will not look favourably on that kind of business. We should do one thing or the other; either take these boats away and put them somewhere else and let the other people go on as they did before, or, if we find that there is enough business to warrant competition, discontinue the subsidy. It is an old theory that the moment a water route becomes so profitable that it can stand competition, the subsidy must go. I thought that principle was always recognized by the Government, and if the minister finds that there is enough business for our boats as well as those of this company, let him drop the subsidy.
We cannot drop the subsidy because this is a passenger service.

The minister should let the item stand until we can have the benefit of the advise of the Minister of Marine, who is in charge of shipping affairs as subordinate to the Minister of Railways, who is in turn under the Board of Management. We should wait until we can get some information to see if this line of ships is really competing with us, and if the subsidy is any longer necessary. This item amounts to about $1,000 per day, which is a good deal of money in these times for the Canadian people to pay, especially when they are paying something

like $200,000 a day of a loss on the Canadian National railways. I think the minister should let the item stand until we can see whether there is not some way by which we can save this $1,000 a day.

I do not think there is any reason for allowing the item to stand. This is a vote which we must have; we must keep that service up; otherwise the whole business would fall to pieces. The boats on this route carried pretty nearly $10,000,000 worth of export freight.
What is the necessity of maintaining this service when vessels of the Canadian Merchant Marine are available?

The vessels of the Canadian Merchant Marine could not carry on the service at all; they are entirely freight vessels. This is a freight and passenger line, and we must preserve it if we are going to maintain communication between Canada and these islands.
Why not utilize the Canadian Merchant Marine when two of its vessels are also being fitted up for this line?
Not this line.
Then what line is it?
That is. another line running from Canada to the Bahamas, Jamaica and British Honduras, an altogether different line.

I am very much inclined to agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Cahill) with regard to this particular item. It seems to me that when we are spending $340,000 a year subsidizing boats for a service to the West Indies, and when vessels of the Canadian Merchant Marine make thirty-two trips, apparently, to the same ports that these vessels serve, we might very well effect some economy here.
Not to the same ports; they are thousands of miles apart.

That may be true, but you have now about thirty-nine vessels in the Canadian Merchant Marine and you are about to increase that number to sixty. It seems to me to be inconsistent, and very bad business, to be building vessels for the Canadian Merchant Marine which will have all they can do to operate at a profit if they, go on this service, and at the same time subsidizing other lines that will compete with us. It would appear that there is not proper co-ordination between the department of my right hon. friend, and

the Department of Marine and Naval Affairs. Under the circumstances, and until we get some explanation from the Minister of Marine that will clear up the uncertainty about this matter, I think the item ought to stand.

At
what ports in South America do the vessels on this service touch?
These vessels do not run to South American ports.
Yes, they go to Deme-rara.
Yes, they do touch at Demarara.
That is a South American port.

The minister stated that a trade of $10,000,000 had been developed. Now, I understand this is a passenger line. How many passengers are represented in that $10,000,000? I do not see the necessity for subsidizing passenger service when it is freight we are looking for, and when we have our own freight ships tied up owing to lack of cargoes. The explanation given by the minister is not very illuminating-it does not explain anything. I regret that the member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) is not in his seat. I am sure that if he were here to-night he would express very strong opposition to this policy of granting subsidies for this purpose. I think, therefore, the minister should let this item stand and give my hon. friend from Red Deer an opportunity of condemning the Government for its extravagance.
The $10,000,000 was the value of the export freight carried. In addition there were a number of passengers amounting to something over three thousand.
And we pay about $100 apiece for carrying these passengers.
We are carrying freight as well as passengers.

But our own ships are tied up in port waiting for freight to carry. Apparently our own ships are capable of carrying this freight, so we do not need to subsidize this passenger service. What benefit is it to us? Would it not be better for us to do away with this subsidy and let our own vessels attend to whatever freight business there is?

You might do away with the subsidy but you would also do away with our West Indian trade in so far as the agreement between ourselves and the West Indies is concerned. If my hon. friend were to look into the matter he would not entertain the idea that you could do away with this passenger and freight service. Unfortunately, our own vessels do not carry passengers. If our own vessels had the necessary passenger accommodation there would be no question about employing them, but they do not and there is the difficulty.

Item agreed to.
Canada and South Africa, steamship service between, $146,000.
That is the usual vote.

I would like to have some information about this item. To say "This is the usual vote" is a very poor explanation for these huge expenditures. Are we getting any value for the money? Is it any benefit to the country? Are we getting fifty cents on the dollar, or ten cents on the dollar, or any value at all for our money? We are voting these large amounts from year to year and the minister says in regard to each of them, "It is the usual vote." To say that it is "the usual vote" might perhaps have been satisfactory when we had lots of money, but it is not satisfactory now when we have unusual taxation. The people of this country are sufficiently burdened without our passing large expenditures on any such ground.

If the vote was there before, it is pretty good proof that it was supposed by Parliament to be necessary, and the necessity does not seem to have diminished. Last year about $10,000,000 worth of exports was carried from our country by that route to South Africa. It is the only subsidized service we have between the two countries. During the last ten years our trade with South Africa has greatly improved. Our merchants are largely availing themselves of this service; in fact it is the only traffic line that they can avail themselves of to get to the South African market. The service might be dropped, but our whole trade with South Africa might then be diverted to some other country.
What is our principal trade with South Africa?
I have told my hon. friend that the vessels on this service carried exports to the value of $10,585,000.
I suppose the products are principally manufactured products that we are now paying the equivalent of a bonus to have manufactured?	.
Yes. It is quite necessary that everything they manufacture should be sold. It is part of our trade.
It is not necessary that the people of Canada should be taxed to find an outlet for the goods of the manufacturer; that is the business.
Yes.

We tried that with Rou-mania. We not only furnished the goods but we paid for them and sent them over there to give the manufacturers something to do. We are taking entirely too much interest in Mr. Manufacturer. He is perfectly capable of taking care of himself, much more so than the farmer or the labouring man who has to pay these subsidies to support the manufacturer. The manufacturer is getting it at both ends; he insists on protection to rob the people here, and not satisfied with that he must rob them again by way of subsidies.
"Rob" is a good strong word.

I know of no stronger
word. If I did I would use it. There is not any more positive robbery in the world than the robbery of the Canadian people by the Canadian manufacturers with the aid of the Government. I think it is about time we took notice of these things. The Government should say to the manufacturers, "Here, these people will some day revolt against this kind of thing."
We take notice of these things every year when we discuss these Estimates and pass them.

We have loaned our gold to every country in the world that cared to borrow it until now we have nothing to base our currency on but cabbages and carrots. But we are not satisfied to buy the manufacturer's goods and sell them to people who will never pay their obligations, we must also provide means for transporting his goods. Do you not think it is time for the people to have a "look-in"

instead of continuing to rob them from day to day? My right hon. friend argues that the point of view of the Government is always right. My experience since I have been in the House is that more often their viewpoint is wrong, and they have had to admit that themselves sometimes. We should stop squandering money to ship the manufacturer's goods for him when he is not in a position to pay himself. Let him look after his own business for awhile.

Does our disadvantage lie in our geographical position or in the incapacity of our manufacturers, or is this subsidy for the purpose of inducing ships to come here and give the manufacturers a cheaper rate? It did not look so serious until the minister said that if we did not vote this subsidy we would lose trade. There must be something wrong somewhere if the holding of this trade is contingent upon the subsidizing of boats to carry our manufactured goods to market.
Does the Government intend putting any of our Mercantile Marine boats on the South African route?
I do not know. The Government may put on some boats to West Africa. This is to South Africa.
I think we should have information.

The export
trade in 1912 amounted to $4,000,000 in round figures, last year to $10,585,000. Our trade has been growing with Africa.
I am not disputing that. I see in 1914 the trade was $3,000,000 and in 1920 it was over $8,000,000. But we should know what is contemplated.

We are putting on our own boats where we can do so. For instance, last year we had a subsidy to a steamship line to Australia amounting to about the same as this. Our own boats have been put on that route and we have withdrawn the subsidy. In so far as our own boats can be substituted to do the work it is our policy to use them.
My right hon. friend is today asking for a subsidy to Australia in the next item $130,000.
That is on the Pacific side.

Item agreed to.

Pacific Ocean. Canada and Australia or New Zealand, or both, on the Pacific Ocean, steam service between, $130,509.

This item appears to be subject to the same criticism I made in regard to the sailings toi the West Indies and South America. There are three proposals here now to establish monthly sailings between Canada and Australia.
The first refers to the service that I spoke of a moment ago from the Atlantic seaports to Australia and New Zealand. That has been taken off.
We are going to establish a service from the Atlantic side by our Government Merchant Marine, and yet subsidize similar services by this vote?

No, not similar services. The service which was carried on for a number of years from the Atlantic ports to Australia and New Zealand was a freight service. For that has been substituted our own vessels, so that subsidy has been withdrawn. On the Pacific side the subsidy I am asking for is contributed by ourselves and New Zealand to a passenger and freight service regularly from Vancouver and Victoria, touching at Fiji and New Zealand and going on to Australia. It is a first-class service. The year before last we gave a subsidy of $180,000, and I have reduced it to $130,000. I should be very sorry to see the subsidy taken away, because I think the service would be withdrawn.
Is this one of the C. P. R. boats?
No, the Union Steamship line.
If the minister would tell us between what ports this service, and the monthly sailings provided by the Department of Marine are to be given, I think we could understand the item.
This line of vessels starts at Vancouver and touches at Victoria.
I am referring to the one on this side.
I am referring to the one on the other side.
I have no trouble with the one on the other side. My hon. friend tells me it is the Atlantic service he is going to subsidize.

My hon. frienl and my other hon. friend thought it was the Pacific side. They are confusing that service with the service on the Atlantic side. We had subsidized for several years a service between the Atlantic ports of Canada and ports in Australia and New Zealand. That subsidy has been dropped, because the Mercantile Marine has put its own vessels on it.

The
mercantile marine propose to put two lines of vessels on the Pacific-monthly sailings direct from Vancouver to Australia and monthly sailings direct from Vancouver to New Zealand. Will that be a similar service to that which my hon. friend now proposes to subsidize?

I do not know the ports at which that service really touches, but if its objective is Australia it will probably touch at Sydney, as is the case with the service proposed to be subsidized.
I do not know whether the ports of call are the same in the case of the New Zealand services.

This is subject to the same criticism as was made in the other case. My right hon. friend is paying his competitor $130,000 to take business away from himself. He should delay the passage of this item until he can consult with the Minister of Marine and ascertain whether or not this subsidy can be dispensed with, as was done in the case of the Atlantic service.

The vessels operated by the Canadian Mercantile Marine on the Pacific are exclusively freight vessels. If we are to have a first-class ser-' vice between Canada and Australia and New Zealand we must have vessels equipped to carry passengers as well as freight.
Do the vessels of the mercantile marine on the Atlantic carry passengers?
No.

Some
of them are equipped to carry passengers. I know that one left Halifax a few days ago with passengers.

Not on that
route. The two vessels which have been fitted up for passenger service go to Jamaica, Nassau and British Honduras.

There should have been a thorough agreement between the Minister

of Marine and the Minister of Trade and Commerce as to the new routes which were to be established. Will the minister say that he was consulted about the various new services which are to be operated by the government-owned boats?

I assure my
hon. friend that I am not running the mercantile marine.

Then what has been
said by the member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) is quite right, that there should be a clear understanding between the Minister of Marine and the Minister of Trade and Commerce on these subjects.
My hon. friend must remember that the classes of vessels in these respective services are different. One is freight solely; the other must be first class passenger and freight.

These services are all for the one people and I do not think it is proper that two departments should act in' dependently when the business is practically the same. Our purpose is to carry trade from Canada to the outside world and vice versa, and if that is to be done by government-owned boats we should not subsidize companies to do the same work. There should be no unnecessary expenditure of the people's money.

It would be
very much easier if the classes of vessels were the same.

How
many boats does the subsidized company propose to operate in this service?

They make a
voyage every four weeks, the ports of call being Vancouver, Victoria, Honolulu, Fiji Islands, Auckland, and a port in Australia.

How many passengers do
they carry?

In 1919 they
carried 9,521. The value of export freight carried was $5,305,000.

This line has been
subsidized for quite a number of years, I believe, and so fas as the minister has told us there is no complaint of congestion of freight or inability on the part of the service to carry what was offered. If we are getting the necessary service as the result of this subsidy, why put our own boats on the same service when we could use them elsewhere with advantage? We

need boats on the St. Lawrence to carry coal to points where it is much needed. Here is a service which is strictly for our own people, and for which a crying need is felt. I see nothing in the proposals of the Minister of Marine which would indicate that any provision is being made for a service of that kind. He does seem to be very solicitous, however, about Australia, New Zealand, and other countries. If the minister can disperse with those far- [DOT] away voyages and put those vessels on serviceable routes in the very heart of our own country, that is what our people will approve more than speculating where or not they shall get any trade on the Pacific in New Zealand, Australia or any of those far-away ports. The principle seems to be that these boats must be put out of sight somewhere or the people will find fault.
I _ wish to bring to the notice of the minister something I discovered within the last two days that I did not know" before.
I find that Norwegian boats which used to carry coal from Nova Scotia to Montreal and St. Lawrence ports are almost prohibited from entering into the trade at all by an Order in Council that was passed in 1902, and although the situation was relieved by an Order in Council which permitted those boats to run, I understand that the last Order in Council permitting them was passed in 1915; and it expired in 1916, so that to-day a Norwegian boat cannot carry on coastal trade in Canada, and it will be very difficult for our coal dealers to get ships to carry their coal.

Those ships
cannot do coastal trade in Canada?

They cannot carry a
pound of freight from one Canadian port to another Canadian port. When we are carrying coal from North Sydney to Montreal, that is, of course, from one Canadian port to another. They cannot handle that trade. Therefore, it is highly important that our boats should do the business-I am not suggesting that they do it for nothing-as cheaply as possible and put us on an independent footing, so that our companies can make contracts with Quebec, Montreal and other places, knowing that they will always have the steamers to carry the coal. The minister is, perhaps, not aware that this is the situation to-day.
I have made inquiries of the Marine and Customs Departments within the last two days, and I was positively informed tonight, that no Norwegian boat, nor any

other foreign boat, can carry freight between any one port and another in Canada.
Unless they reciprocate with our vessels. I suppose that is the principle.

That is the situation
now. We have nothing to send to Norway, and there is nothing to do after we get there, so that reciprocity would be of no good to us. I am very glad, for one thing, that we have those ships, and I am sure the minister will keep in mind, in co-operation with the other department, that that is the best service in which they can 'be used.

My hon. friend (Mr. Mc-
Kenzie) has spoken a number of times about those ships and about the St. Lawrence coal trade. He referred to the matter several days ago in the House. I think I am not going too far when I tell my hon. friend that I have it on very credible authority that those ships that he speaks of as being tied up in different ports, are now under repairs and being refitted for the coal trade of the coming summer, and that they are now under contract and will likely be in the coal trade carrying coal from Sydney Harbour to Montreal and the different St. Lawrence ports.

That answers
the question of my hon. friend.

I am glad that the
hon. member has come to the assistance of the minister. My right hon. friend did not know what was going on in his department. Now we have it on the highest possible authority that certain repairs are going on and possibly some contracts will be entered into.
My hon. friend ought to be satisfied.

Another feature of this matter that I do not think the minister has looked into is the enormous expense he will incur in running this service to New Zealand and Australia by these large Governement boats if there is no trade for them. If it is true that the service that we now have is able to carry the goods that are passing between Vancouver and Australia and New Zealand, why are we proposing now to put on five 8,000-ton boats to compete with the service that we are now subsidizing? This is what the Minister of Marine and Fisheries says:
Vancouver-Australia and New Zealand service. Established February 23, 1920: Monthly sailings: Allotted five 8,100-ton steamers: These
steamers call, East and West bound, at Wellington, Auckland, Sydney and Melbourne.
The expenditure of running these five large steamers between Vancouver and Australia will be enormous. They have to plough their way through the Pacific ocean burning coal that will cost some six dollars a ton. You cannot expect them to run for a day with less than fifty tons of coal, so that that amounts to $300. Therefore, the five boats will take at least $1,500 worth of coal per day to keep them running on the Pacific ocean, and the coal is only a small item compared with wages and other expenses to keep these steamers in commission. This looks to me like an insane proposal unless the minister can show an enormous increase in trade between Vancouver and those ports in Australia and New Zealand. The Marine Department are proposing to put those five large government owned boats on that service, the Minister of Trade and Commerce is proposing to subsidize * the old service that carried the trade before, and we have no information at all to show us that there is any need of putting those new boats on. The minister ought to take my advice and stop asking for the passing of this item until he consults the Minister of Marine' and Fisheries in order to find out just where he stands in regard to this matter.

In answer to a question
I asked, the minister stated that some 9,000 passengers were carried from Vancouver to Australia. Did he mean that the subsidized boats had carried 9,000 passengers?
Yes.

Did he also mean that the
$5,000,000 worth of goods shipped from Canada to Australia was carried by those boats?
Yes.
What is the tonnage of those boats?

Some of the boats that run
to Australia are first class ships of ten, twelve and fifteen thousand tons. Our ships are not in the same class.

The tonnage
of the Makura is gross, 8,200 and the Niagara, 13,444.
Our ships are 8,100 tons.
Yes.
Item agreed to.
Mail subsidies and steamship subventions- local services-Mulgrave and Canso, steam service-between, *$13,500.
Has this contract been renewed for the coming year?
I think it has. It will be anyway.

Item agreed to.
Pictou, Montague, Murray Harbour, and Georgetown, steam service between, $6,000.
Has this service been renewed?
I am not sure, but it is about the time for signing the contract.

Item agreed to. /
Supervision of subsidized steamship services, expenses in connection with, $4,000.

Before we dispose of this last item I would like to remind my right hon. friend that last session I called his attention to what I supposed was an accident in the omission of a small subsidy of $1,000, I think the amount was for the steam service between the town of Lock-port and Froude's Point. It is a service between the Canadian National railways and the town of Lockport. My right hon. friend said that he had dropped it out as he understood it was merely a ferry of three-quarters of a mile, speaking from memory. I pointed out that that was quite a mistake. By road it is four or five miles, and by water four miles. It is really an important service. It is not a question of subsidizing any company, for the service is maintained by the town of Lockport, and if there is any deficiency the town has to make it up by taxing the people. I think it is as legitimate a claim as many of these here of the same class. I am quite sure that my right hon. friend was mistaken on the ground on which he left this item out, and I draw his attention to the matter now in the hope that when the Supplementary Estimates are being prepared he will be able to make provision for it. It is not a question of subsidizing any private capitalist or anything of that sort. It is a service run by the town of Lockport, and is of vital importance to them and also to the Canadian National railways. Lockport is one of the largest towns on the south coast, and is a very important fishing community. It is already doing a large fishing business, and would do a much greater business if it had better transportation

facilities. My right hon. friend cannot introduce an item now, but I trust he will make a note of it and make provision for this service in the Supplementary Estimates.
I will certainly look into it.

Civil Government

Patent & Copyright- Salaries, $161,292.50 ; contingencies, $35,000.
Is this increase of almost $29,000 justifiable?

The increase is due largely to the reclassification. Then there are some additional appointments which are necessary in order to clear up the arrears of work which have accumulated during the latter years of the war. Extra examiners have to be appointed for the largely increased number of applications for patents. While the war was on, there were not so many applications, but now the applications are in arrears and piling up, and when people pay for patents they want them got out. I have very carefully gone over this vote, and I can assure my hon. friend there are no unnecessary additions to the staff. ^
Are we doing something this session with regard to copyright? Is ther a Bill under consideration?
There is a Bill under way.

Item agreed to.
